X-Splat: Unified Gaussian Splatting for Joint RGB and X-ray 3D Reconstruction

SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 Conference Papers; December 01–04, 2026; Kuala Lumpur, MalaysiaConference: SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 Conference Papers (SA Conference Papers ’26), December 01–04, 2026, Kuala Lumpur, MalaysiaDOI: 10.1145/3829340.3842177979-8-4007-2842-6/2026/12ISBN: Computing methodologies Point-based modelsCCS: Computing methodologies ReconstructionCCS: Wangze Xu , Affiliation: The University of TokyoJapanemail: xwz@g.ecc.u-tokyo.ac.jp, Chu Zhou , Affiliation: National Institute of InformaticsJapanemail: zhou_chu@pku.edu.cn, Mae Yamaguchi , Affiliation: The University of TokyoJapan, Linrui Dai , Affiliation: The University of TokyoJapan, I-Chao Shen , Affiliation: The University of TokyoJapan, Takashi Ijiri , Affiliation: Shibaura Institute of TechnologyJapan and Imari Sato , Affiliation: National Institute of InformaticsJapan, Affiliation: The University of TokyoJapanemail: imarik@nii.ac.jp© cc

Abstract.

Jointly reconstructing RGB and X-ray provides new insights by connecting external appearance with internal structure, enabling a more complete understanding of real-world objects than single modality. Yet existing methods train separate models per modality and suffer from redundant geometry, alignment artifacts, and loose coupling that limits cross-modal insight discovery. We propose a unified representation in which all Gaussian primitives share a single set of geometric parameters, with only surface-proximal primitives additionally carrying appearance attributes. We perform cross-modal registration through clean multi-view stereo and X-ray geometric proxies instead of aligning two sets of optimized Gaussians, improving alignment stability. We then jointly optimize the unified representation via supervision from both modalities, complemented by a surface-depth consistency loss derived from X-ray geometry to guide RGB reconstruction. Experiments on the InsideOut dataset and our dataset show that our framework achieves more robust cross-modal alignment, higher RGB rendering quality without compromising X-ray reconstruction, and a more compact representation than maintaining two independent geometries. Project page: .Flower & Insecthttps://zezeaaa.github.io/X-Splat/

3D Gaussian splatting, cross-modal 3D reconstruction, X-ray tomography, novel view synthesis

Keywords:

†by†cc-license:

1.

Real-world objects are both surface and interior: we readily see a flower’s outer petals, but not the structure within. Yet existing 3D reconstruction typically captures only one of the two at a time. RGB cameras record the external appearance through surface reflection, while X-ray imaging penetrates objects to reveal their internal volumetric structure through attenuation, leaving the two as separate digital records of the same physical object. We pursue a unified 3D representation that natively captures both, enabling consistent rendering of an object’s exterior and interior from any viewpoint (Fig. ). Such a unified representation supports applications such as digital cultural heritage , industrial inspection , and physically-grounded visualization , providing a more complete understanding of real objects than either modality alone.1()Bossema et al., 2024()Bergmann et al., 2019()Ni et al., 2024

Existing 3D reconstruction work has developed each modality along a separate track. RGB-based approaches built on neural radiance fields (NeRF)  and Gaussian splatting  reconstruct external surfaces but treat the object interior as unobserved space. X-ray-based methods such as NAF , X-Gaussian , and R-Gaussian  recover internal density distributions but provide no surface appearance. Training separate models per modality is a natural starting point, yet such a decoupled approach keeps two independent representations of the same object with no cross-modal alignment, increasing parameter count and preventing consistent rendering of external appearance and internal structure.()Mildenhall et al., 2021()Kerbl et al., 2023()Zha et al., 2022()Cai et al., 2024a2()Zha et al., 2024

A more principled direction is to design a single framework targeting RGB and X-ray jointly, and the recent InsideOut  is the first such attempt. It trains a separate Gaussian set per modality and bridges them through hierarchical alignment between the two optimized representations. While this design takes a first step toward joint reconstruction, it leaves several aspects underexplored. First, the two Gaussian sets independently model the same underlying geometry, doubling the parameter footprint. Second, the alignment operates on optimized Gaussian primitives that are the outcome of geometric and appearance fitting rather than a faithful description of the object’s surface, and contain floaters and optimization artifacts, leading to surface-to-interior misalignment that compromises applications requiring aligned internal-external display, such as digital cultural heritage . Finally, although the scene geometry is accurately recovered from X-ray, it is still underutilized in RGB optimization, leaving RGB weakly supervised and limiting surface fidelity in applications such as industrial inspection .()Lee et al., 2025()Bossema et al., 2024()Bergmann et al., 2019

To address these limitations, we present , a unified Gaussian framework for joint RGB-X-ray 3D reconstruction. Our design is based on a simple observation: although RGB images arise from surface reflection and X-ray images from volumetric attenuation, both are ultimately conditioned on the geometry of the same physical object. This shared geometric origin suggests that the cleanest design is not to model each modality with its own independent geometry, but to let the two modalities share a single geometric representation while specializing only the attributes that genuinely differ between them. Concretely, we propose a unified Gaussian representation in which all primitives share a single set of geometric parameters, and only primitives close to the surface carry appearance attributes, reflecting the physical fact that RGB observations arise primarily from surface reflection. This eliminates the redundancy of maintaining two independent geometries and lets gradients from both modalities flow into the same shared geometry. To bring the two modalities into a common coordinate frame, we register them through clean geometric proxies derived directly from the input data, namely a multi-view stereo (MVS)  point cloud from the RGB views and a mesh extracted from the X-ray reconstruction, rather than aligning the already-optimized Gaussians. Finally, we exploit the shared geometry to enable joint optimization across both modalities, complemented by a surface-depth consistency loss using X-ray-derived surface geometry to supervise RGB rendering. In summary, our contributions are:X-Splat(; ; ; ; )Yao et al., 2018Gu et al., 2020Yang et al., 2020Peng et al., 2022Cao et al., 2022

  • •

    with shared geometric parameters and surface-restricted appearance attributes, enabling compact joint modeling of external appearance and internal volumetric structure.A unified Gaussian representation

  • •

    using clean MVS and X-ray proxies to register two modalities, avoiding the surface-to-interior misalignment that arises when registering two sets of already-optimized Gaussians.A geometry-based alignment pipeline

  • •

    where both modalities update shared parameters via their respective objectives, complemented by an X-ray-derived surface-depth consistency loss.A joint optimization scheme

    • We evaluate on the InsideOut dataset  and a new dataset combining existing flower scans  with newly captured insect specimens, broadening evaluation to natural objects. Our method achieves more robust cross-modal alignment, better RGB rendering quality without compromising X-ray reconstruction, and is more compact than two independent models.X-Splat()Lee et al., 2025Flower & Insect()Ijiri et al., 2014

    2.

    External Appearance Reconstruction

    Neural radiance fields (NeRF) have substantially advanced the appearance reconstruction of 3D objects from RGB images, which established a differentiable volume-rendering paradigm that fits a continuous radiance field to multi-view images. Subsequent work improved its rendering quality and efficiency through multi-scale anti-aliasing  and hash-grid encodings . A parallel line replaces the volumetric formulation with neural implicit surfaces  to recover sharper geometry. More recently, 3D Gaussian Splatting  represents the scene with explicit Gaussian primitives and a tile-based rasterizer, achieving real-time rendering at comparable visual quality, with Mip-Splatting  addressing aliasing under varying sampling rates. Subsequent work has improved surface fidelity by reformulating the primitives as 2D disks  or regularizing them toward the underlying surface . Other lines extend to sparse-view , pose-free , and dynamic  settings. While these methods achieve high-quality external appearance reconstruction, the internal structure of objects remains beyond their scope.()Mildenhall et al., 2021()Barron et al., 2021()Müller et al., 2022(; )Wang et al., 2021Yariv et al., 2021()Kerbl et al., 2023()Yu et al., 2024()Huang et al., 2024()Guédon and Lepetit, 2024(; ; ; ; ; )Deng et al., 2022Wang et al., 2023Li et al., 2024bZhu et al., 2024Xu et al., 2024Peng et al., 2024(; ; ; ; )Fan et al., 2024Fu et al., 2024Shen et al., 2024Ye et al., 2025Wang et al., 2025(; ; ; ; ; ; )Fridovich-Keil et al., 2023Yang et al., 2024Wu et al., 2024Qian et al., 2024Hu et al., 2024Xu et al., 2025Zhan et al., 2025

    Internal Structure Reconstruction

    X-ray and computed tomography (CT) reconstruction  recovers the internal density distribution of an object from projection measurements. Classical analytical methods such as FDK  remain the standard for cone-beam CT, producing volumetric reconstructions in closed form when projections are dense. To handle sparse-view settings, NAF  adapts a neural attenuation field to fit projection measurements with a continuous network representation, and SAX-NeRF  employs a line-segment Transformer to capture spatial structure from X-ray projections. More recently, Gaussian splatting has been extended to the X-ray modality. X-Gaussian  replaces alpha-compositing with a radiative rasterizer that follows the Beer-Lambert law, enabling efficient X-ray novel-view synthesis. R-Gaussian  further corrects an integration bias in this rasterization formulation and introduces a differentiable voxelizer that enables accurate tomographic reconstruction. Subsequent work also explores direction-disentangled volume rendering for realistic radiographs . While these methods achieve high-quality internal density reconstruction, external surface appearance lies beyond the X-ray modality.(; ; )Gordon et al., 1970Li et al., 2023Yu et al., 2025()Feldkamp et al., 1984()Zha et al., 2022()Cai et al., 2024b()Cai et al., 2024a2()Zha et al., 2024()Gao et al., 2024

    Cross-modal 3D Reconstruction

    3D reconstruction has long benefited from auxiliary modalities captured by physical sensors that complement RGB cameras. Depth sensors such as LiDAR and commodity time-of-flight devices provide direct geometric measurements that supplement photometric supervision in driving  and indoor scenes . Thermal and infrared imaging extend RGB reconstruction to scenarios invisible to RGB cameras, with recent work introducing implicit neural fusion of far-infrared and RGB imagery . Multi-spectral and hyperspectral cameras likewise enrich RGB reconstruction with material- and wavelength-specific signals . Recent Gaussian-splatting frameworks further model RGB jointly with thermal images , or with multiple modalities through shared and modality-specific Gaussian components . These auxiliary modalities all carry surface-domain signals, leaving the reconstructed target on the externally observable surface. Few works have attempted to combine external appearance with internal structure. Joining RGB and X-ray for 3D reconstruction differs fundamentally, since they arise from different physical mechanisms. Prior combinations of the two modalities operate at the image level in medical image fusion  or serve geometric calibration between the two sensing systems , and learned priors have been used to predict unseen object thickness from RGB-D observations . None of these produces a unified 3D representation of appearance and internal structure. The most relevant prior work is InsideOut , which hierarchically fits two independently optimized Gaussian sets and bridges them by a post-hoc visual alignment. In contrast, we align via purely geometric registration and adopt a unified representation with shared geometric parameters, enabling truly joint optimization.(; )Rematas et al., 2022Sun et al., 2024()Keetha et al., 2024(; )Li et al., 2024aHassan et al., 2024(; )Thirgood et al., 2025Meyer et al., 2025()Lu et al., 2025()Gu and Wang, 2025()Nair and Singh, 2018()Albiol et al., 2016()Nicastro et al., 2019()Lee et al., 2025

    3.

    Imaging Formation: Reflection vs. Transmission

    RGB and X-ray imaging differ fundamentally in how light interacts with matter. In RGB imaging, most of the radiance received along a camera ray originates near the first surface it encounters on an opaque object, and the observed pixel intensity is modeled as the integral of emitted color along the ray, weighted by accumulated transmittance,

    (1)Irgb(𝐫)=∫tntfT(t)α(𝐫(t))c(𝐫(t))dt,T(t)=exp(−∫tntα(𝐫(s))ds),I_{\mathrm{rgb}}(\mathbf{r})=\int_{t_{n}}^{t_{f}}T(t)\,\alpha\bigl(\mathbf{r}(t)\bigr)\,c\bigl(\mathbf{r}(t)\bigr)\,dt,\>T(t)=\exp\!\left(-\int_{t_{n}}^{t}\alpha\bigl(\mathbf{r}(s)\bigr)\,ds\right),

    where and are the volumetric opacity and color fields, and are the near and far bounds of the ray, and is the transmittance from the camera to depth . In contrast, an X-ray penetrates the object along its entire path, and the log-domain pixel value is the line integral of the density field along the ray, governed by the Beer–Lambert law,α⁡(⋅)\alpha(\cdot)c⁡(⋅)c(\cdot)tnt_{n}tft_{f}T⁡(t)T(t)ttσ⁡(⋅)\sigma(\cdot)

    (2)Ixray​(𝐫)=∫tntfσ⁡(𝐫⁡(t))​𝑑t.I_{\mathrm{xray}}(\mathbf{r})=\int_{t_{n}}^{t_{f}}\sigma\bigl(\mathbf{r}(t)\bigr)\,dt.

    Despite these distinct optical mechanisms, both modalities observe the same underlying object, and each is a different forward operator acting on a common 3D geometry.

    3D Gaussian Representation

    Datasets.

    We evaluate our method on two datasets covering nine scenes. The first is the InsideOut dataset , which provides four scenes (Matryoshka, Pharaoh, Skull, and Toy Gun) with paired RGB photographs and ground-truth CT volumes. The second, which we refer to as the dataset, contains two flower scenes (Tulip, Eustoma) from  and three insect scenes (E02, E15, E32) acquired from prepared specimens, all with paired CT volumes. To evaluate all baselines under identical X-ray acquisition geometry, we follow the protocol of R-Gaussian  and re-synthesize cone-beam projections from ground-truth CT volume using TIGRE , sampling 50 training and 120 testing projections uniformly over at resolution. After Stage 1 we extract the CT mesh, recover the geometry-based alignment (Sec. ), and construct the surface set with surface distance threshold and reference opacity . Stage 2 then jointly optimizes the unified representation for iterations under , , and . Each photometric loss combines with D-SSIM at and . The CT mesh is re-extracted every iterations during Stage 2, and is computed on virtual cameras sampled by Fibonacci sphere. All other hyperparameters follow 3DGS defaults ; complete settings, learning rates, and densification thresholds are listed in the supplementary material. Training takes approximately – minutes per InsideOut scene on a single NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU. As the official InsideOut  implementation is not publicly available, we reproduce their method by following the descriptions and hyperparameters reported in their paper. [Extension=.otf,ItalicFont=lmromandemi10-oblique]lmromandemi10-regular MirroS Technical Report [Blog][Code][Project Page][Code worlds for evolving agents. : Diverse environments spanning distinct geometries, visual appearances, and interactive tasks. : Agents continuously evolve through environmental interactions, developing increasingly sophisticated strategies such as shelter-building and ramp-crossing.]\pdfauthor\metadatahttps://mirros.ai/blog/worlds-for-evolving-agents\metadatahttps://github.com/MirroS-Lab/AgentGarten\metadatahttps://mirros-lab.github.io/agent-garten\teaserfigure\captionleadfontTopBottom

AgentGarten: Code Worlds for Evolving Agents

MirroS Technical Report October 8, 2026

Abstract

Interactive virtual worlds allow agents to learn through exploration and interaction. What agents can learn is bounded by the environments they practice in, which must be , with consistent state, rules, and dynamics, and , with observations that follow the real-world visual distributions. Achieving both across diverse worlds remains a bottleneck. We introduce , a framework that couples simulators and game engines with a shared to build real-time interactive environments. Its simulation backends maintain persistent world state and execute program-defined interaction rules, while the renderer generates visual observations from structured conditions exported through a common interface. To build the neural renderer, we adapt a pretrained video model to geometry conditions, distill it with our proposed , and optimize inference for real-time interaction. Adversarial Forcing makes history prefilling differentiable through exact replay, so that losses on later predictions update how the renderer encodes prior observations, and adds real-data adversarial supervision to improve its visual quality. In AgentGarten, agents perceive the world through visual observations, interact with it in real time, and improve by distilling each round of experience into playbooks that subsequent agents inherit and refine. Our empirical study demonstrates a substantial gain in learning efficiency, with agents learning from just 4 rounds compared with millions for a conventional reinforcement learning counterpart. As new worlds can be written as code and rendered through the same interface, environments can scale in both number and difficulty alongside their agents, a step toward agents that keep evolving through interactive experience.faithfulrealisticAgentGartenneural rendererAdversarial Forcing

world models, code worlds, executable environments, neural rendering, autoregressive video generation, distribution matching distillation, agents

keywords

1

Agents learn from trajectories of actions and observations. Developing scalable, generalizable agent capabilities requires environments that not only faithfully preserve the consequences of past actions over extended interactions, but also support flexible variation in layouts, objects, and task rules. Across navigation, manipulation, and multi-agent interaction, scaling these environments therefore requires both controllable, inspectable dynamics and diverse visual observations.

However, existing approaches face a fundamental trade-off. Simulators and game engines support agent learning through explicit state and programmable interaction rules . Yet expanding their visual diversity entails substantial 3D asset creation and complex rendering pipelines, making new environments costly to build and customize. Conversely, video world models synthesize rich, interactive visual observations from data . In these models, however, task-relevant state and physical transition rules remain implicit within generated histories and learned representations, precluding direct inspection, editing, and testing of the environment’s behavior.[, , ]123[, , , ]4567

We introduce , a framework for building that combines programmable dynamics with a shared, real-time neural renderer (Figure ). In AgentGarten, each scene program runs in a simulator or game engine that maintains persistent state and executes explicit interaction rules. A shared neural renderer synthesizes the agent’s visual observations from structured conditions exported by the engine through a unified interface. This separation preserves rigorous control over state and rules while allowing compatible engines to share a single renderer. New environments can thus be authored by coding agents from text or image inputs, then edited and extended entirely in code without creating bespoke visual assets for every scene.AgentGartencode worlds1

Operating a video model as an interactive neural renderer requires it to strictly follow updated engine conditions, maintain visual consistency across extended rollouts, and synthesize observations in fine-grained, short blocks so that agents receive immediate feedback after brief actions. We adapt a pretrained bidirectional video model to structured conditions, convert it to block-causal generation, and distill it into a real-time renderer on a single GPU with , which trains the renderer on its own rollouts via distribution matching and introduces two key advances. First, to allow later losses to update the history-encoding computation without the memory cost of a fully differentiable rollout, we adopt two-pass training and introduce : a block-by-block execution schedule that eliminates numerical divergence between sampling and recomputation and achieves bitwise-identical recomputation of the rollout trajectory. Second, to prevent the visual degradation that score distillation alone exhibits over long rollouts, we incorporate a real-data adversarial objective and derive an exact R1/R2 regularization scheme for a discriminator with a frozen backbone, entirely avoiding double-backward passes through fused attention kernels.Adversarial Forcing[, , ]8910[]11exact replay[, ]1012

Code worlds provide rich environments for agents to practice and evolve. We evaluate pretrained foundation-model agents across rounds of interaction, where they perceive the world strictly through rendered observations, diagnose failures, and distill key insights into written inherited by subsequent rounds. In hide-and-seek , agents rapidly grounded abstract spatial knowledge into closed-loop physical execution, with ramp use and shelter construction emerging within a handful of games. The same reflective loop improved performance across rounds in several additional, diverse environments (Section ).playbooks[]135

Our contributions are: {contributions}

A framework for code worlds that couples persistent, editable environment state to a shared real-time neural renderer through structured conditions, enabling programmable interaction and diverse visual observations across compatible engines without per-scene visual asset authoring.

, a distillation method for a few-step, block-causal neural renderer. It combines distribution matching on self-rollouts with exact bitwise replay for history gradients, alongside a real-data adversarial objective whose exact R1/R2 regularization avoids double-backward through fused attention.Adversarial Forcing

An empirical study of evolving agents. Pretrained agents observing exclusively through neural rendering rapidly ground semantic tool knowledge and improve outcomes across rounds through written playbooks in hide-and-seek and several further distinct worlds.

2

2.1

A code world combines a scene program , an engine that executes it, and a neural renderer . The program specifies the scene and interaction rules. Let denote the scene state, including object poses, articulations, and task variables; the observing camera pose; and the actions of one or more agents. The engine updates the state and captures a structured condition from the camera:ppRθR_{\theta}sts_{t}πt\pi_{t}ata_{t}ctc_{t}

(st+1,πt+1)=fp​(st,πt,at),ct=hp​(st,πt),(s_{t+1},\pi_{t+1})=f_{p}(s_{t},\pi_{t},a_{t}),\qquad c_{t}=h_{p}(s_{t},\pi_{t}),(1)

where implements the state transition and renders the visible geometry. Given an appearance reference and a text description , the neural renderer generates subsequent observations from visual history :fpf_{p}hph_{p}x0x_{0}yyx<tx_{<t}

xt=Rθ​(x<t,c≤t,x0,y),t≥1.x_{t}=R_{\theta}\!\left(x_{<t},\,c_{\leq t},\,x_{0},\,y\right),\qquad t\geq 1.(2)

The agent receives and selects , which determines the next state and condition through Eq. ().xtx_{t}ata_{t}1

Unlike a video world model, whose state resides in generated history, the transition takes no rendered observation as input: the renderer influences the state only through the actions that agents select, so rendering errors cannot accumulate in the state. A recorded state trajectory can consequently be rendered again under a different appearance reference or camera without altering the underlying events. Conversely, the renderer observes the state only through ; attributes that the conditions leave undetermined, such as color and material, are specified by and and carried by the visual history. The renderer consumes conditions and visual history in blocks, as described in Section .fpf_{p}c≤tc_{\leq t}x0x_{0}yy3

2.2

We use colorized depth or surface normals as structured conditions. Both can be estimated from video or rendered by an engine, and their three-channel representation allows us to reuse the pretrained video encoder and Transformer. For real videos, we obtain depth with ViPE , using Depth Anything 3  as its depth backend, and normals with NormalCrafter . Simulated scenes supply these maps directly from geometry, without requiring detailed materials or textures. During training, each sample uses one randomly chosen modality (Section ).[]14[]15[]163.2

We encode depth with the Vision Banana mapping  and camera-space unit normals as , using consistent coordinate and orientation conventions across estimated and rendered maps (Appendix ).[]17(n+1)/2(n+1)/2A.2

2.3

A coding agent constructs a code world from either a single image or a text description, producing an executable scene program along with an appearance reference . Because appearance is delegated to the neural renderer, the scene program does not require detailed materials or leaf-level assets; it only needs coarse geometry that faithfully conveys layout, silhouettes, occlusion, and motion dynamics.x0x_{0}

From an image.

The input image serves simultaneously as and the reference layout (Figure ). Perception and generation models lift the visible content into instance masks , monocular depth and camera intrinsics , 3D bounding boxes , and extracted object meshes . When building from text, the agent writes the scene program directly using geometric primitives and engine assets. Code worlds give agents many places to act, and a world that answers every action is also a place to practice. This section presents environments built on the shared renderer, revisits hide-and-seek with agents that perceive the world only through rendered observations, describes the round-by-round procedure through which they improve, and applies it to four further worlds.

AgentGarten: Code Worlds for Evolving Agents

MirroS Technical Report October 8, 2026

Abstract

Interactive virtual worlds allow agents to learn through exploration and interaction. What agents can learn is bounded by the environments they practice in, which must be , with consistent state, rules, and dynamics, and , with observations that follow the real-world visual distributions. Achieving both across diverse worlds remains a bottleneck. We introduce , a framework that couples simulators and game engines with a shared to build real-time interactive environments. Its simulation backends maintain persistent world state and execute program-defined interaction rules, while the renderer generates visual observations from structured conditions exported through a common interface. To build the neural renderer, we adapt a pretrained video model to geometry conditions, distill it with our proposed , and optimize inference for real-time interaction. Adversarial Forcing makes history prefilling differentiable through exact replay, so that losses on later predictions update how the renderer encodes prior observations, and adds real-data adversarial supervision to improve its visual quality. In AgentGarten, agents perceive the world through visual observations, interact with it in real time, and improve by distilling each round of experience into playbooks that subsequent agents inherit and refine. Our empirical study demonstrates a substantial gain in learning efficiency, with agents learning from just 4 rounds compared with millions for a conventional reinforcement learning counterpart. As new worlds can be written as code and rendered through the same interface, environments can scale in both number and difficulty alongside their agents, a step toward agents that keep evolving through interactive experience.faithfulrealisticAgentGartenneural rendererAdversarial Forcing

world models, code worlds, executable environments, neural rendering, autoregressive video generation, distribution matching distillation, agents

keywords

1

Agents learn from trajectories of actions and observations. Developing scalable, generalizable agent capabilities requires environments that not only faithfully preserve the consequences of past actions over extended interactions, but also support flexible variation in layouts, objects, and task rules. Across navigation, manipulation, and multi-agent interaction, scaling these environments therefore requires both controllable, inspectable dynamics and diverse visual observations.

However, existing approaches face a fundamental trade-off. Simulators and game engines support agent learning through explicit state and programmable interaction rules . Yet expanding their visual diversity entails substantial 3D asset creation and complex rendering pipelines, making new environments costly to build and customize. Conversely, video world models synthesize rich, interactive visual observations from data . In these models, however, task-relevant state and physical transition rules remain implicit within generated histories and learned representations, precluding direct inspection, editing, and testing of the environment’s behavior.[, , ]123[, , , ]4567

We introduce , a framework for building that combines programmable dynamics with a shared, real-time neural renderer (Figure ). In AgentGarten, each scene program runs in a simulator or game engine that maintains persistent state and executes explicit interaction rules. A shared neural renderer synthesizes the agent’s visual observations from structured conditions exported by the engine through a unified interface. This separation preserves rigorous control over state and rules while allowing compatible engines to share a single renderer. New environments can thus be authored by coding agents from text or image inputs, then edited and extended entirely in code without creating bespoke visual assets for every scene.AgentGartencode worlds1

Operating a video model as an interactive neural renderer requires it to strictly follow updated engine conditions, maintain visual consistency across extended rollouts, and synthesize observations in fine-grained, short blocks so that agents receive immediate feedback after brief actions. We adapt a pretrained bidirectional video model to structured conditions, convert it to block-causal generation, and distill it into a real-time renderer on a single GPU with , which trains the renderer on its own rollouts via distribution matching and introduces two key advances. First, to allow later losses to update the history-encoding computation without the memory cost of a fully differentiable rollout, we adopt two-pass training and introduce : a block-by-block execution schedule that eliminates numerical divergence between sampling and recomputation and achieves bitwise-identical recomputation of the rollout trajectory. Second, to prevent the visual degradation that score distillation alone exhibits over long rollouts, we incorporate a real-data adversarial objective and derive an exact R1/R2 regularization scheme for a discriminator with a frozen backbone, entirely avoiding double-backward passes through fused attention kernels.Adversarial Forcing[, , ]8910[]11exact replay[, ]1012

Code worlds provide rich environments for agents to practice and evolve. We evaluate pretrained foundation-model agents across rounds of interaction, where they perceive the world strictly through rendered observations, diagnose failures, and distill key insights into written inherited by subsequent rounds. In hide-and-seek , agents rapidly grounded abstract spatial knowledge into closed-loop physical execution, with ramp use and shelter construction emerging within a handful of games. The same reflective loop improved performance across rounds in several additional, diverse environments (Section ).playbooks[]135

Our contributions are: {contributions}

A framework for code worlds that couples persistent, editable environment state to a shared real-time neural renderer through structured conditions, enabling programmable interaction and diverse visual observations across compatible engines without per-scene visual asset authoring.

, a distillation method for a few-step, block-causal neural renderer. It combines distribution matching on self-rollouts with exact bitwise replay for history gradients, alongside a real-data adversarial objective whose exact R1/R2 regularization avoids double-backward through fused attention.Adversarial Forcing

An empirical study of evolving agents. Pretrained agents observing exclusively through neural rendering rapidly ground semantic tool knowledge and improve outcomes across rounds through written playbooks in hide-and-seek and several further distinct worlds.

3.5

The renderer prefills the reference and text, denoises incoming blocks, and commits clean predictions into a bounded KV cache. The cache maintains a permanent prefix (including ) and a sliding window of recent history (Figure ). For rollouts exceeding the training horizon, we apply top-aligned rotary position remapping: the active block is clamped at the horizon boundary while recent history is shifted to precede it and re-rotated, preserving relative temporal distances while geometry tracks the true simulation timeline (Appendix ).sinkx0x_{0}6C

Low-latency execution and deployment.

Transformer execution over short blocks is primarily bounded by memory bandwidth and kernel launch overhead. Rather than relying on , which incurs minutes-long cold-start compilation delays, we implement custom Triton kernels to fuse elementwise operations around attention (RMSNorm, RoPE rotation, and gated activations) without intermediate memory round-trips. CUDA graph capture and replay further eliminate host-side launch overhead for fixed-shape blocks. To bypass the heavy latent decoding bottleneck during real-time serving, we optionally replace the standard VAE decoder with a distilled tiny decoder , which reconstructs pixel frames in under 10 ms (Table ). In interactive deployments, the engine pushes conditions to a GPU worker, and decoded frames are streamed to the agent or browser over WebRTC with bounded queuing latency (Section ).torch.compile[]29[]30[]3124.3

4

4.3

With the hand-written kernels, CUDA graph capture, and the tiny decoder (Section ), the renderer generates video at over 35 frames per second on one NVIDIA H100 GPU, including condition encoding, four denoising steps, decoding, and host transfer. Table  breaks one served block of sixteen frames into its parts. The cache keeps five sink and 44 recent latent frames, one of the history windows used in distillation (Appendix ), so each four-frame block attends to 49 frames of history. The block is measured at steady state with the cache full: blocks 17 to 48 of a 48-block, 769-frame rollout, averaged over two rollouts. Attention is dense and the tiny decoder runs in FP16.3.5480×832480\times 8322C

5

Code worlds give agents many places to act, and a world that answers every action is also a place to practice. This section presents environments built on the shared renderer, revisits hide-and-seek with agents that perceive the world only through rendered observations, describes the round-by-round procedure through which they improve, and applies it to four further worlds.

item.title: Does Tile Granularity Matter? An Empirical Study of Vector Tile Compression for Map Rendering with MapLibre Tiles

Five heterogeneous geospatial datasets were encoded as conventional tile pyramids and as tw

License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.25755v1 [cs.DB] 19 Oct 2026

Vector Tile Compression for Map Rendering with MapLibre Tiles

Does Tile Granularity Matter? An Empirical Study of Vector Tile Compression for Map Rendering with MapLibre Tiles

Viacheslav Nefedov Ivan Nefedov Petr Datsenko Samuil Datsenko Ariel University Affiliation: Holon Institute of Technology Affiliation: Technion Affiliation: Middle East Technical University Affiliation: 

Abstract

Vector tiles are the display format of interactive maps: clients download the tiles that cover the current view and render their content themselves. Their compactness matters for storage, offline use and network transfer, particularly when maps with custom thematic layers are served from constrained hardware or over limited links. Because vector maps are delivered as pyramids of small, independently encoded tiles, the spatial granularity of the encoding unit is set largely by the tiling scheme rather than by the encoding format. We examine how this granularity affects compression in the column-oriented MapLibre Tiles (MLT) format, using Mapbox Vector Tiles (MVT) as a feature-oriented baseline. Five heterogeneous datasets, including a geological map and a wetland inventory, were encoded as a conventional pyramid and as two denser variants that represent the area of and conventional tiles in one independently encoded tile at approximately the same logical level of detail. Moving from the conventional to the variant increased MLT’s raw saving over MVT in all five datasets, by 1.0–7.3 percentage points (pp). After per-tile gzip, the saving increased in four datasets by 1.5–6.4 pp and decreased in one by 1.4 pp. Coarser granularity made MLT streams longer in every dataset, and the gain was largest where conventional tiling produced the shortest streams: across datasets, as the mean number of values per stream in conventional tiles rose from 27 to 2,075, the raw gain fell monotonically from 7.3 to 1.0 pp. Larger units reduced structural overhead per encoded value and, most clearly in two datasets, the encoded payload cost per value. For the two sparse datasets, coarser units also reduced bytes per vertex for every encoding, and the archives were 71% and 33% smaller than the conventional ones with MLT and gzip. The measured advantage of a column-oriented vector-tile format therefore depends on the spatial granularity at which it is evaluated, and conventional fine-grained tiling can understate its compression potential.2×22\times 24×44\times 44×44\times 44×44\times 4

1

Interactive maps are drawn on the client from tiles. The map is cut into a pyramid of zoom levels and, at every level, into a regular grid; each tile is encoded, stored and transferred independently, and the client requests the tiles that cover its current view and styles and renders their content itself . Vector tiles are therefore a display format: they carry geometry and attributes already selected and generalized for drawing at one scale, not the source data from which they were derived. The compactness of this representation matters well beyond download time. It determines the storage cost of map archives that cover the whole planet, the feasibility of offline maps on mobile devices and in low-connectivity settings, and the volume of data that clients must transfer and decode. These pressures grow with the underlying data. OpenStreetMap passed ten billion nodes in August 2025 , and as early as 2024 the Overture Maps release combined 2.35 billion building footprints from OpenStreetMap, Esri Community Maps and machine-learning extractions by Microsoft and Google .(; )OpenStreetMap Wiki, n.d.bMasó and Jacovella-St-Louis, 2022()OpenStreetMap Wiki, n.d.c()Overture Maps Foundation, 2024

This study grew out of practical work with maps of this kind. In a commercial fleet-management system for ground robots that operate in remote areas with little or no connectivity, the on-site server, a computer of the Raspberry Pi class, also serves maps to the operator. The operator views the area with custom layers that depend on the robot’s task, such as agricultural work, clearing vegetation under power lines or snow removal. A similar need arises in a student project for the NASA International Space Apps Challenge on the visualization of planetary surfaces, which NASA itself distributes as web map tiles . Both settings display custom thematic layers, which are often sparse, from stored tile archives, consider MLT as the encoding, and are constrained by storage, link capacity or computing power. Neither system uses the results reported here, and no data from them enter the experiment. They raised the question that this paper studies in isolation: how far the tiling scheme, rather than the encoding format, limits how compactly such maps can be stored and delivered.()NASA, n.d.b()NASA, n.d.a

The dominant encoding for vector tiles has been the Mapbox Vector Tile (MVT) format , which stores each feature as a Protocol Buffers message that holds its geometry and its attributes; in this sense MVT is feature-oriented. MapLibre Tiles (MLT) is a recently proposed successor that reorganizes tile content into columns: geometry and each attribute are stored in separate streams and compressed with lightweight encodings such as dictionary, run-length and delta encoding and integer bit-packing . Column-oriented layouts with such encodings are well established in analytical databases and data lakes , and spatial variants have been proposed for geospatial data lakes .()Mapbox, 2016(; )Tremmel and Zink, 2025MapLibre, 2026c(; ; )Abadi et al., 2006Zeng et al., 2023Kuschewski et al., 2023()Saeedan and Eldawy, 2022

The efficiency of columnar encoding, however, depends on how much data each independently encoded unit contains. Every stream carries structural information, and lightweight encodings have more opportunity to exploit regularity when a stream contains more values. In columnar storage this dependence is well known and is controlled explicitly: Apache Parquet lets the writer choose the size of row groups and data pages, and its documentation notes that larger pages carry less header overhead and recommends large row groups .()Apache Software Foundation, n.d.a

We use in a specific sense: the geographic area and corresponding content grouped into one independently encoded tile at an approximately fixed logical level of detail. This is distinct from , the integer coordinate grid used inside a tile; from , measured in bytes; and from the rendered tile size in screen pixels. In a conventional pyramid the spatial granularity is imposed by the tile matrix rather than chosen by the encoding format. The MVT specification deliberately keeps bounds and projection outside the tile ; the quadtree pyramid, in which each zoom level doubles the linear resolution, comes from tiling conventions shared by servers and renderers . Generalization policies keep tiles small as well, since production tilers drop or simplify features to bound tile size. In a measurement of seven production web maps (Appendix ), the vector tiles we observed were typically only a few kilobytes on the wire, with per-product medians between 0.1 and 3.8 KB.spatial tile granularitycoordinate extentencoded tile size()Mapbox, 2016(; )OpenStreetMap Wiki, n.d.bMasó and Jacovella-St-Louis, 2022A

Seen from the display client, this fixed unit appears smaller than necessary. Three observations from the settings above led us to the present question. First, the rendered tile size is fixed: MapLibre GL JS draws vector tiles at 512 CSS pixels , so at an integer zoom level a viewport of CSS pixels, the one used in Appendix , intersects 20 to 30 tiles at once. The client thus already holds a block of several tiles for a single view. Second, typical map tasks, such as surveying an area to choose a site for equipment, span several screens and several zoom levels, so a session requests many more tiles than one view: in Appendix , a session of two pans and one zoom step loaded between about 270 and 770 tiles in six of the seven products. These two observations suggest that a coarser encoding unit need not cost much additional transfer, although we do not measure that cost here (Section ). Third, and most important, the density of map content varies widely between tiles, whereas at a given zoom level every tile covers the same area. Dense urban tiles are already large, while tiles of sparse thematic layers hold a handful of features and consist largely of per-tile structure. Because the unit is fixed by the tile matrix, an encoder cannot enlarge it where the content is sparse. In our own map applications we have worked around this limit with overzoom and by combining several tilesets with different maximum zoom levels; such workarounds reduce the number of tiles but do not change the unit of compression in a controlled way (Section ).()MapLibre, 2026b2560×16002560\times 1600AA52.2

That larger blocks of data compress better is unsurprising in itself. Less obvious is how strongly a columnar tile format depends on spatial encoding-unit granularity compared with a feature-oriented one, and whether the effect survives general-purpose transport compression such as gzip . The original MLT evaluation reports compression up to three times better than MVT across tilesets and more than six times better for some large tiles . MapLibre’s current planet-scale benchmarks make the association more explicit: naturally large tiles obtain larger MLT gains than median tiles . Those results stratify existing tiles by observed encoded size; they do not manipulate the spatial boundary of the independently encoded unit while holding logical level of detail approximately fixed.(; )Deutsch, 1996aDeutsch, 1996b()Tremmel and Zink, 2025()MapLibre, 2026d

Prior work has also varied vector-tile partitioning, zoom, pyramid depth and tile content, but these interventions either change level of detail together with spatial scale, optimize content within a fixed tile, or change pyramid organization rather than the compression-unit boundary . To our knowledge, no previous study has systematically varied the spatial granularity of independently encoded vector tiles under approximately matched-content, matched-LoD conditions and quantified the resulting raw and per-tile-gzip size of column-oriented MLT relative to feature-oriented MVT.(; ; ; ; )Li et al., 2018Dufilie and Grinstein, 2014Bahadori and Eldawy, 2026Felt, n.d.Planetiler contributors, 2026

In this paper we study this interaction empirically. We encode five heterogeneous datasets, ranging from global small-scale reference data to large-scale national topography, as a conventional tile pyramid and as two denser variants in which each tile represents the content of a or group of conventional tiles, with the coordinate extent increased to preserve spatial precision. These variants are an experimental device: standard clients cannot display them directly, but they correspond to encoding units of a quarter of a desktop view to roughly a whole view, and they emulate such units while keeping both encoders unchanged. For every variant we compare paired MVT and MLT tiles, as encoded and after gzip, and relate the differences to tile content and to the internal stream structure of MLT. We address four research questions:2×22\times 24×44\times 4

  • RQ1

    How does tile granularity affect the size saving of MLT over MVT, as encoded and after gzip?

  • RQ2

    Which characteristics of tile content predict this saving?

  • RQ3

    Which stream-level mechanism in MLT is consistent with the observed effect?

  • RQ4

    Does coarser granularity reduce the number of bytes per vertex for both general-purpose (gzip) and columnar (MLT) compression?

    • We make the following contributions:

  • 1.

    An empirical comparison of MLT and MVT across three tile granularities on five heterogeneous datasets and 36,647 tile instances, evaluated as encoded and after gzip, together with an openly available processing pipeline and per-tile statistics (Sections  and ).34.1

  • 2.

    Evidence that tile content predicts raw saving strongly in four of the five datasets, and that across all five datasets the Standard mean values per MLT stream ranks the raw granularity gain exactly in reverse order (Section ).4.2

  • 3.

    A stream-level characterization showing that coarser granularity lengthens MLT streams and reduces non-payload structural overhead in every dataset, while aggregate encoded payload bytes per value also decrease from Standard to Dense-16 in all five datasets (Section ).4.3

  • 4.

    A format-independent comparison in bytes per vertex showing that, for sparse datasets, coarser granularity benefits feature-oriented, columnar and gzip compression alike (Section ).4.4

    • The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section  introduces vector tiling schemes, the MVT and MLT formats and related work. Section  describes the datasets, the tiling variants and the metrics. Section  presents the results, Section  discusses their implications for tiling-scheme design, and Section  examines threats to validity.23456

    2

    This section introduces the concepts the study relies on: how tiled vector maps are organized (Section ), how practitioners already depart from the conventional tile pyramid (Section ), how MVT and MLT lay out the content of a tile (Section ), and why the size of an independently encoded unit matters for compression (Section ). Section  positions the study with respect to prior work.2.12.22.32.42.5

    2.1

    Web maps are not delivered as a single file. The world is divided into square tiles at a series of zoom levels, and a client downloads only the tiles that cover its current view ; with vector tiles the client also styles and draws their content itself. At zoom 0 a single tile covers the world, and each level splits every tile into four, so a complete level  contains tiles. A tile is addressed by its zoom, column and row, written , and archives such as PMTiles map each address to a stored tile . More general tiling schemes, with other projections and tile matrices, are standardized by the OGC Two Dimensional Tile Matrix Set , but the quadtree scheme above is the one used by almost all web vector maps. Figure  summarizes these concepts.()OpenStreetMap Wiki, n.d.bzz4z4^{z}z/x/yz/x/y()Protomaps, n.d.()Masó and Jacovella-St-Louis, 20221

    Each zoom level is generated for its own scale. At low zoom levels only major features are kept and their shapes are simplified, while deeper levels add smaller features and finer detail (Figure ). A tile is therefore a summary of its area at one scale rather than the union of its four children. Production tile generators also bound the size of each tile: Tippecanoe, for example, by default limits a tile to 500 kB of compressed data and 200,000 features, lowers the resolution of tiles that exceed the size limit, and offers options to drop or coalesce features .2()Felt, n.d.

    Inside a tile, geometry is stored as integer coordinates on a local grid, the , conventionally 40964096 units . The tile does not record its own position: its address is kept outside the tile, and the tile format itself does not prescribe a pyramid . Every tile is encoded independently, so an encoder can exploit repetition only among the features of one tile, and each tile repeats its own layer, column or stream structure.extent×\times()Mapbox, 2016z/x/yz/x/y(; )Mapbox, 2016MapLibre, 2026f

    We distinguish four quantities that are easily conflated. is the geographic area and corresponding content grouped into one independently encoded tile at a given logical level of detail. is the integer grid used to represent coordinates inside that tile. is the resulting number of bytes. is the screen-space size used by a client. Increasing coordinate extent alone changes precision, not spatial granularity; in our experiment it is increased together with spatial aggregation so that the coarser encoding unit retains approximately the same coordinate precision.Spatial tile granularityCoordinate extentEncoded tile sizeRendered tile size

    2.2

    The dense quadtree pyramid is the default, but practitioners already depart from it, mainly to reduce the number of stored tiles and requests.

    Overzoom.

    A client may display a tile at zoom levels deeper than the deepest level stored, scaling the tile up instead of requesting its children. The extent is the main limit on this practice: the extent field of MVT is an unsigned 32-bit integer whose value 4096 is a default rather than a maximum , and MLT declares the extent per layer and notes that a larger extent gives more precision at the cost of more bytes . Developer proposals build on this. A MapLibre proposal argued that “using a large tile extent allows you to tile your dataset only as far as is necessary” ; a Planetiler feature request asks for an extent of 16384 at the maximum zoom so that a small tileset can be overzoomed, instead of raising the maximum zoom, which would greatly increase the archive size ; and Tippecanoe can add extra detail at the maximum zoom to improve precision when overzooming . On the client side, MapLibre GL JS now splits a deep-overzoomed source tile into virtual child tiles in a worker and overscales only the last few levels, by default four .()Mapbox, 2016()MapLibre, 2026f()Loer, 2023()Agafonkin, 2025()Felt, n.d.()MapLibre, 2026a

    Metatiles.

    Raster tile servers commonly render and store , usually blocks of tiles, because rendering one large area is cheaper than rendering many small ones, labels are placed more consistently, and fewer files need to be stored . Metatiles are a server-side unit, however: clients still request and receive individual tiles.metatiles8×88\times 8()OpenStreetMap Wiki, n.d.a

    Larger tiles.

    Vector tile services have also offered larger tiles directly. The Tilezen service (formerly Mapzen) served 256- and 512-pixel tiles, stating that a single 512-pixel request is equivalent to four 256-pixel requests, and listed fewer requests, better label placement, smaller files and less disk space for offline use among the advantages of the larger size . The 512-pixel vector tile has since become the convention of WebGL renderers such as MapLibre GL JS .()Tilezen, n.d.()MapLibre, 2026b

    Sparse pyramids.

    Tippecanoe can generate a variable-depth pyramid that omits child tiles wherever the parent is detailed enough to be overzoomed . A corresponding Planetiler proposal asks for variable tile depth so that descendants need not be generated where an ancestor already represents the required detail . Archives such as PMTiles can store such sparse pyramids, but clients need a way to distinguish a tile that is intentionally missing, and should be replaced by an overzoomed ancestor, from one that is empty. A design proposal for MapLibre adds this distinction to tiled sources and TileJSON .()Felt, n.d.()Planetiler contributors, 2026()MapLibre contributors, 2026a

    The rendered tile.

    These approaches increase how much information a stored tile carries, but not the size of the unit that the client renders: MapLibre GL JS, for example, requires vector sources to use a tile size of 512 pixels . Their motivations are primarily rendering precision, storage and request count. They do not provide a controlled measurement of compression as a function of the spatial boundary of one independently encoded unit. The denser variants studied here apply a related idea at every logical zoom: a tile covers the area of multiple conventional cells while a larger coordinate extent preserves approximately the same spatial precision.()MapLibre, 2026b

    2.3

    The Mapbox Vector Tile (MVT) format encodes a tile as a Protocol Buffers message with named layers. Each layer holds a sequence of feature records; a record contains the feature’s geometry, written as integer drawing commands with zigzag-encoded coordinate deltas, and its attributes, written as indices into tables of keys and values shared by the layer . The layout is thus feature-oriented (Figure a), and redundancy across features is exploited mainly through the shared key and value tables and, in practice, by gzip applied to the whole tile.()Mapbox, 20163

    MapLibre Tiles (MLT) organizes vector-tile content by column . Within a layer, each property of all features, such as geometry type, vertex offsets, vertex coordinates or an attribute, is stored as a column, and each column is split into of same-typed values, for example presence, data, length and offset streams. Every stream carries its own metadata, namely the number of values, the byte length and the encoding . Streams are compressed with lightweight encodings such as dictionary, run-length and delta encoding combined with integer packing, chosen per stream by the encoder (Figure b). The original evaluation reports compression up to three times better than MVT over whole tilesets and more than six times better for some large tiles . MapLibre’s public benchmarks on two planet-scale basemaps report smaller gains after gzip: the stable MLT v1 reduces gzipped archive size by about 15% for OpenMapTiles and 5% for Protomaps, and the experimental MLT v2 by about 18% and 10% . The same benchmarks show that disabling a dictionary shared by several columns enlarges the uncompressed archive by about 25% for one of the two basemaps , an indication of how much the format depends on redundancy that exists within one tile. Unlike MVT’s per-feature property types, MLT declares one type per property column within a layer of a tile; mixed input types therefore require normalization during conversion .(; )Tremmel and Zink, 2025MapLibre, 2026cstreams()MapLibre, 2026f3()Tremmel and Zink, 2025()MapLibre, 2026d()MapLibre, 2026d()MapLibre, 2026e

    2.4

    The dependence of compression on the amount of data in one encoding unit is well known outside cartography. Column stores compress data well because values of one column are stored together and lightweight encodings can be applied to long runs of similar values , and empirical studies of Parquet and ORC show that the choice and effectiveness of encodings depend on the data within each unit . These formats expose the unit size as a parameter. Parquet lets the writer choose the size of row groups and data pages; its documentation notes that larger pages carry less header overhead and recommends row groups of 512 MB to 1 GB . ORC divides files into stripes of typically about 200 MB and compresses streams in chunks of 256 kB by default, noting that larger chunks compress better at the cost of memory . Spatial Parquet carries these ideas over to geospatial data lakes .()Abadi et al., 2006(; )Zeng et al., 2023Kuschewski et al., 2023()Apache Software Foundation, n.d.a()Apache Software Foundation, n.d.b()Saeedan and Eldawy, 2022

    General-purpose compressors show the same dependence. DEFLATE, the algorithm behind gzip, finds repetitions within a sliding window of 32 kB , so data that repeat across separately compressed files cannot be exploited. The Zstandard documentation describes this as the small-data problem: the smaller the input, the harder it is to compress, because at the start of a new input there is no past to build upon, and it offers trained dictionaries, whose gains are concentrated in the first few kilobytes, as a remedy .(; )Deutsch, 1996aDeutsch, 1996b()Meta Platforms, n.d.

    A vector tile differs from these settings in two ways. Its encoding unit is small, typically kilobytes rather than megabytes (Appendix ), and its spatial granularity is not a free parameter of the encoder: it follows from the tile matrix and the generalization policy. Coordinate extent can be configured independently, but it controls the local coordinate grid rather than the geographic area of the encoded unit.A

    2.5

    Prior work approaches this question from several adjacent directions. The original MLT evaluation compares MLT and MVT on existing tiles and reports especially large gains for some large tiles . MapLibre’s current planet-scale benchmarks go further and explicitly show that naturally large tiles benefit more from MLT . These are important precedents, but tile size is an observed property of the corpus: the spatial boundary of the independently encoded tile is not manipulated.()Tremmel and Zink, 2025()MapLibre, 2026d

    Other studies manipulate quantities that are related to granularity but confound it with another change. GeoTile reports compressed vector-tile sizes across zoom levels, where spatial footprint changes together with feature selection and level of detail . Feathered Tiles studies adaptive spatial partitioning and targets roughly uniform tile payloads, but does not measure a compression-versus-partition-size curve . HiFIVE systematically reduces byte size by pruning records, attributes and values within a fixed tile, so its intervention is content reduction rather than a change of the spatial encoding unit . Variable-depth pyramids and overzooming in Tippecanoe and Planetiler change which pyramid levels are stored, not the compression boundary at a fixed logical zoom .()Li et al., 2018()Dufilie and Grinstein, 2014()Bahadori and Eldawy, 2026(; ; )Felt, n.d.Planetiler contributors, 2026Agafonkin, 2025

    These distinctions matter because changing zoom, fidelity, pyramid depth or observed payload size does not isolate spatial granularity. To our knowledge, no prior work has systematically varied the area represented by each independently encoded vector tile under approximately matched-content and matched-LoD conditions and quantified the resulting raw and externally compressed size, particularly for column-oriented MLT relative to feature-oriented MVT. Studies of columnar storage establish the general importance of encoding-unit size, but at much larger, non-cartographic block sizes.(; ; ; )Abadi et al., 2006Zeng et al., 2023Kuschewski et al., 2023Saeedan and Eldawy, 2022

    3

    The experiment converts five heterogeneous vector datasets into tile pyramids at three granularities, encodes every pyramid in MVT and in MLT, and compares the paired encodings tile by tile. Preparation is split into two stages: Stage A normalizes each raw source once into a canonical GeoPackage, and Stage B generates all tile variants from that GeoPackage, so that the variants of one dataset differ only in tiling parameters.

    3.1

    The corpus was chosen to cover different ways in which geospatial data are produced, because the production process largely determines how much geometry and how many attributes a map carries per unit area. It contains a generalized small-scale reference map (Natural Earth), a national large-scale topographic register (PDOK), two thematic survey products (USFWS wetlands and the swisstopo geological map) and a crowdsourced dataset (OpenStreetMap). Table  lists their provenance and Figure  shows samples.14

    Processing whole national or global datasets at three granularities exceeded the memory and time available for the GDAL-based pipeline, so each dataset was clipped to a study area (Table ). The areas were chosen to contain dense content for each dataset: the eastern United States for Natural Earth, the Säntis region of north-eastern Switzerland for the swisstopo map, and the same area around New Orleans for both USFWS and OSM. The last choice gives a matched pair: two datasets with very different content over identical geography, which helps to separate the effect of content from that of location.20.4∘×0.4∘0.4^{\circ}\times 0.4^{\circ}

    The datasets differ along the dimensions that matter for a columnar encoder. Natural Earth has few features per unit area but many layers and attributes. USFWS consists almost entirely of one polygon layer with very detailed boundaries, about 210 vertices per feature in the raw source, and few attributes. PDOK is dense in features of many classes with rich attribute schemas. The swisstopo map has few features over a small area. OSM combines dense buildings with sparser lines and points and a very large, sparse tag vocabulary.

    Figure  shows three nested views per dataset from the Standard MVT archives. The stored zoom levels and tile addresses were selected for each map’s characteristic content and fixed in a reproducible region configuration. Square viewports lie inside both the selected tile and the dataset bounds at that zoom; clipped margins outside those bounds are excluded. Magenta outlines mark the next view, while zoom labels and palette explanations are typeset in LaTeX. OSM and USFWS use the same viewports for a direct comparison of coastal Louisiana. Complete tile addresses, viewport bounds, approximate ground sizes and color inventories are exported with the figures.4

    3.2

    Each raw source was converted with GDAL into a canonical GeoPackage in Web Mercator (EPSG:3857) with two-dimensional geometries, clipped once to the study area and indexed spatially. Source layers were mapped onto a common set of semantic kinds (water, land, boundary, transport, place, building, infrastructure, terrain) so that all datasets can be rendered with one style sheet and inspected visually. Several source layers can be merged into one tile layer, which gives between one (USFWS) and ten (PDOK) tile layers per dataset (Table ). For Natural Earth, which has 183 source layers with heterogeneous schemas, only a common subset of attributes (feature class, names in four languages, administrative codes and rank fields) was kept. Geometry is not altered by this mapping. A manifest records the source and rule hashes, CRS, bounds, layer counts, feature identity strategy and GDAL version, so that every normalized layer can be traced back to its source.2

    The grouping of source layers into tile layers affects the absolute size of both encodings, and of MLT in particular, because it determines how many features share one set of streams. The mapping rules are identical for all variants of a dataset and for both encodings. However, changing tile granularity can change which property types co-occur within an output layer, so the resulting type conversions are measured separately (Section ).3.5

    3.3

    MVT tiles were generated with the GDAL MVT driver (GDAL 3.13.3, official container image), written to MBTiles and repacked into PMTiles archives . We did not use Planetiler, a common tile generator, because its output extent is fixed at 4096 units and making it configurable is still an open request ; the denser variants require extents of 8192 and 16384. The GDAL driver exposes the extent, the buffer, the simplification tolerance and per-layer zoom ranges as parameters. Simplification was the same for all variants, 1.6 tile units below the maximum zoom and 1.0 at the maximum zoom. Because the tolerance is expressed in tile units, it corresponds to the same ground distance at the same level of detail in every variant. The buffer was units, the same fraction (about 2%) of the tile width in every variant. The driver’s limits on tile size and feature count, by default 500 kB and 200,000 features, were set to the largest possible value (), so that no features were dropped or written at reduced precision. Logical zoom ranges are listed in Table ; individual tile layers start at zoom 2 to 7 depending on their content.()GDAL/OGR contributors, n.d.()Protomaps, n.d.()Agafonkin, 202580⋅2d80\cdot 2^{d}231−12^{31}-12

    3.4

    Three variants were generated from each normalized dataset (Figure , Table ). We operationalize as the area, and therefore the amount of approximately matched-LoD content, grouped into one independently encoded tile. With detail offset , one stored tile covers the area of Standard cells at the same logical level of detail.54spatial tile granularityd∈{0,1,2}d\in\{0,1,2\}4d4^{d}
