来源：arXiv·cs.GR 最新（English） 相关度：14.6 正文：35118 字 / 3 图

命中：texture、lighting、mesh、relight

Single image 3D generation aims to dress a given 3D mesh with relightable materials while faithfully preserving the visual details of a reference image. Existing methods either introduce artifacts when fusing inconsistent multi-view predictions or struggle to preserve fine details through implicit image-feature conditioning. To resolve these challenges, we introduce SUPRA-Tex, built on the princip

SUPRA-TEX:

Chen YangJiemin FangFanpeng MengZihao HuangAffiliation: Huawei Inc.Jichen PangGuanjun WuZhikuan BaoQi TianAffiliation: Huawei Inc.Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong UniversityAffiliation: Huazhong University of Science and Technology*Equal contributionAffiliation: Project leadAffiliation: Corresponding authors

1  Introduction

For applications such as product digitization and embodied AI, generating relightable 3D assets from a single reference image requires faithful preservation of the reference appearance. We refer to this requirement as super-alignment: accurately reproducing fine-grained text, logos, and patterns at their corresponding visible surface locations, while completing unobserved regions with materials consistent with the visible appearance.

Two prominent approaches to appearance generation are multi-view synthesis and native 3D generation. Multi-view pipelines leverage geometry-conditioned 2D generative models to synthesize appearance across surrounding viewpoints, then project and fuse the resulting images onto the mesh (Tencent Hunyuan3D Team, 2025b). However, cross-view discrepancies can introduce seams and ghosting, while blending conflicting predictions blurs sharp reference details ; (Lai et al., 2026Zeng et al., 2026).

Native 3D generation circumvents view-fusion artifacts by synthesizing appearance directly on 3D representations ; ; ; (Lai et al., 2026Chen et al., 2026Zeng et al., 2026Xiang et al., 2026), yet preserving fine reference details remains challenging. For example, TRELLIS.2 employs a 3D material VAE to compress surface PBR properties into material latents, which are generated under geometry and image conditioning before being decoded into surface materials. Its image cross-attention provides no explicit correspondence between image details and 3D surface locations, leaving the generator to learn where those details belong. To improve spatial alignment, recent work lifts high-resolution image features into 3D through camera projection (Li et al., 2026a). Yet even with explicit spatial correspondence, these conditions remain visual features rather than material observations. Consequently, the 3D generator must simultaneously shoulder the responsibilities of inferring PBR properties from visual features, reconstructing fine reference details at their corresponding surface locations, and synthesizing materials for unobserved regions.

We argue that these responsibilities should not fall on a single 3D generator. Given the inherent scarcity of 3D training data, requiring the 3D model to learn these heterogeneous tasks jointly increases its learning burden. Instead, we offload visible-material estimation to 2D generative priors and establish explicit surface alignment through camera projection, separating both from the 3D generative task. Our key insight is to translate visible reference evidence into native material observations before 3D generation, then organize full-surface completion around this grounded evidence. Rather than forcing the 3D model to infer physical materials from abstract visual features, this formulation enables the generator to anchor directly on established material evidence, preserving reference details while focusing more of its capacity on completing unobserved surfaces.

Based on this principle, we introduce SUPRA-Tex, a framework for generating relightable 3D assets with super-aligned textures. First, we leverage strong 2D priors by training an MLLM-based image editing model to jointly predict lighting-separated PBR maps in the reference view in a single forward pass, while preserving fine visual details. Next, we project these maps onto valid visible surface locations and encode the resulting partial materials with the pretrained material VAE encoder into native observation latents. Sharing the target latent space and directly decodable by the pretrained material decoder, these latents provide spatially aligned material content rather than abstract visual features that the 3D backbone must translate into PBR properties. We also encode the spatial extent of these observations to guide completion.

To guide full-surface material generation, we design an interleaved flow transformer that reads the native observation latents as fixed, read-only reference memory at every block. Its blocks alternate between updating unobserved latent cells and the full surface, allocating more updates to cells without observations while retaining full-surface interactions for coherent completion. Since observations are indexed by 3D surface coordinates, the same interface incorporates additional views, including 2D-generated back views, and interactive 2D edits without retraining the 3D backbone. Through this division of labor, SUPRA-Tex delivers What You See Is What You Get fidelity in the reference view while completing the asset with globally coherent, relightable materials, as illustrated in Fig. .

Using only public datasets for training, SUPRA-Tex achieves SOTA results in both geometry-conditioned texturing and end-to-end asset generation. With synthetic back-view conditioning, SUPRA-Tex achieves reference fidelity and visual quality on real photographs comparable to or better than those of the leading commercial systems in our comparisons. Code and checkpoints are released on our project page to facilitate future research: supra-3d.github.io/supratex.

Our main contributions are as follows:

  • •

    Our key insight is to establish surface-aligned material observations before 3D generation, allowing the generator to focus on preserving reference details and completing unobserved surfaces. Built on this insight, SUPRA-Tex is trained solely on public datasets and, with synthetic back-view conditioning, achieves reference fidelity and visual quality comparable to or better than those of leading commercial systems in our comparisons.

  • •

    We present native observation encoding, which projects reference-view PBR estimates onto valid surface locations and encodes partial materials in the target latent space, simplifying learning to preserve reference appearance.

  • •

    We propose an interleaved flow transformer that uses fixed, read-only observation anchors and alternates unobserved-cell and full-surface updates for reference-faithful, coherent material completion.

    • 2  Related Work

    Multi-view texture generation. Most texturing pipelines synthesize appearance in 2D views and fuse the predictions onto the mesh. Early approaches paint the mesh view-by-view with depth-guided diffusion and inpaint unobserved UV regions ; ; (Richardson et al., 2023Chen et al., 2023Zeng et al., 2024a). TexFusion aggregates view-wise denoising predictions in a shared latent texture map (Cao et al., 2023). Subsequent works improve cross-view coherence by synchronizing multi-view denoising ; ; (Liu et al., 2024bCheng et al., 2025Bensadoun et al., 2024) or generating views jointly via geometry-conditioned diffusion ; ; ; ; (Huang et al., 2025bShao et al., 2025Liang et al., 2026Han et al., 2026Zhang et al., 2026), a recipe also adopted by large image-to-3D systems ; ; (Zhang et al., 2024aLi et al., 2025bTencent Hunyuan3D Team, 2025a). Reference-guided methods also explicitly target appearance preservation: EASI-Tex combines mesh-edge guidance with image features for single-image texturing (Perla et al., 2024), while AlignTex aligns multi-view artwork with the mesh before projection and texture refinement (Zhang et al., 2025b). Optimization-based approaches such as DreamMat distill geometry- and light-aware diffusion priors into PBR materials (Zhang et al., 2024b). Paint-it instead optimizes convolutionally parameterized PBR texture maps with score distillation (Youwang et al., 2024). To produce relightable assets, multi-view generation is extended to PBR channels using lighting-aware priors, material latent representations, or alternating view-space baking ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; (Deng et al., 2024Huang et al., 2025aHe et al., 2025aYeo et al., 2026Feng et al., 2025Tencent Hunyuan3D Team, 2025bLai et al., 2025Bao et al., 2026Wu et al., 2026b), often aided by single-image intrinsic delighting ; ; ; ; ; (Kocsis et al., 2024Zeng et al., 2024bKe et al., 2025Chen et al., 2024He et al., 2025bCareaga and Aksoy, 2024). Nevertheless, residual inconsistencies between synthesized views can blur or ghost sharp reference details during projection and blending. In contrast, SUPRA-Tex completes materials in native 3D space, using projected observations as conditioning anchors rather than directly fusing synthesized views into the final texture.

    Native texture generation. Driven by the rise of large-scale 3D pretraining, native texture generation has emerged as an alternative paradigm. Existing approaches explore diffusion over point, octree, and UV representations ; ; (Yu et al., 2023Liu et al., 2024aYu et al., 2024) and PBR prediction with octree-aligned Gaussians (Xiong et al., 2025). Latent texture generators, such as NaTex, LaFiTe, and TEXTRIX, learn structured latent spaces for surface colors or attributes ; ; (Lai et al., 2026Chen et al., 2026Zeng et al., 2026), while native 3D foundation models jointly represent geometry and appearance ; ; (Chen et al., 2025Xiang et al., 2025Xiang et al., 2026). Beyond global conditioning, partial observations and spatially aligned features have also been explored. At scene scale, WorldGrow (Li et al., 2026b) extends TRELLIS with context-conditioned 3D block inpainting for progressive scene generation. TEXGen back-projects partial UV maps (Yu et al., 2024), NaTex encodes initial textures for refinement (Lai et al., 2026), and TEXTRIX encodes projected appearance with its pretrained attribute VAE in the generation target’s latent space (Zeng et al., 2026). For spatial feature alignment, camera projection techniques originally developed for implicit reconstruction ; (Saito et al., 2019Yu et al., 2021a) have been adapted to 3D generative models, such as CUPID’s pose-aligned features and Pixal3D’s camera-frame back-projected multi-scale features ; (Huang et al., 2026Li et al., 2026a). Even with spatially aligned image features, the 3D generator must still infer material properties, preserve reference details, and complete unobserved surfaces.

    3  Method

    Given a reference image II, a mesh ℳ\mathcal{M}, and its camera projection π\pi, SUPRA-Tex generates full-surface, relightable PBR materials. Figure 1 summarizes the three stages: reference-view material estimation, surface-aligned native observation encoding, and observation-guided 3D completion. We first introduce the material representation and upstream geometry model, then describe the three stages, training objective, and inference procedure. Appendices A and B provide implementation and training details; Appendix G.1 describes additional-view conditioning and texture editing.

    3.1  Preliminaries

    Surface PBR and material latents. We represent surface appearance through physically based rendering (PBR) properties over the mesh ℳ\mathcal{M}. At any surface location 𝐩∈ℳ\mathbf{p}\in\mathcal{M}, these properties comprise albedo 𝐚∈ℝ3\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}, metallic m∈[0,1]m\in[0,1], and roughness r∈[0,1]r\in[0,1]. We build on the O-Voxel representation of TRELLIS.2 (Xiang et al., 2026), which additionally includes opacity α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1], giving the material tuple T⁡(𝐩)=(𝐚⁡(𝐩),m⁡(𝐩),r⁡(𝐩),α⁡(𝐩))T(\mathbf{p})=(\mathbf{a}(\mathbf{p}),m(\mathbf{p}),r(\mathbf{p}),\alpha(\mathbf{p})). Separate sparse VAEs compress 3D geometry and surface materials into geometry latents G={gs}s∈𝒮G=\{g_{s}\}_{s\in\mathcal{S}} and material latents Z={zs}s∈𝒮Z=\{z_{s}\}_{s\in\mathcal{S}} over active coordinates 𝒮\mathcal{S}. For sparse surface attributes 𝒫\mathcal{P}, the pretrained material VAE encoder EmatE_{\mathrm{mat}} yields ZZ; conditioned on GG, the material generation stage models PBR materials directly in the native 3D space by generating ZZ, which the decoder DmatD_{\mathrm{mat}} restores onto the mesh surface.

    Geometry foundation and camera projection. Our framework takes a mesh ℳ\mathcal{M} and camera projection π\pi, either provided as ground truth or predicted from the reference image. We use the open-source TRELLIS.2-based Pixal3D variant ; (Li et al., 2026aXiang et al., 2026), denoted Pixal3D⋆, which supports geometry and material generation. Its geometry module predicts the reference-aligned mesh for end-to-end generation.

    3.2  Image-to-Material Translation

    To reduce the learning burden on the 3D generator, we separate reference-view material estimation from 3D surface completion. Specifically, we train an MLLM-based image editing model F2​DF_{\mathrm{2D}} to infer reference-view albedo and metallic-roughness (MR) maps directly from the input photograph:

    T^2​D=F2​D​(I)=(𝐚^,m^,r^),\widehat{T}_{\mathrm{2D}}=F_{\mathrm{2D}}(I)=\left(\widehat{\mathbf{a}},\widehat{m},\widehat{r}\right),(1)

    where 𝐚^\widehat{\mathbf{a}} denotes the albedo map, and m^\widehat{m} and r^\widehat{r} denote the metallic and roughness maps. To reuse the 3-channel pretrained image VAE, we pack m^\widehat{m} and r^\widehat{r} with a constant channel into a 3-channel map, which also fulfills the input format expected by the pretrained material encoder.

    Joint alignment and one-step inference. To coordinate channel predictions while retaining pretrained image priors, F2​DF_{\mathrm{2D}} adapts a multimodal DiT backbone (Super Intelligence Team, 2026) via factorized modality-axis joint attention, jointly predicting albedo, metallic–roughness, and auxiliary normal maps. This attention exchanges features across output modalities at corresponding spatial locations. We train the 2D material estimator on RGB images paired with ground-truth material and normal maps rendered from Objaverse, using a latent flow-matching objective at the fixed maximum-noise endpoint σ=1.0\sigma=1.0. At inference, a single DiT forward pass at this endpoint (1.2 s on one H800) estimates clean material latents, which the VAE decodes into 1024×10241024\times 1024 material maps without iterative denoising.

    This design has two advantages. First, it uses 2D image priors to disentangle illumination from intrinsic materials at full reference resolution. Second, it shields the downstream 3D generator from abstract visual features, letting the 3D model use physical PBR observations to focus on reference preservation and unobserved-surface completion.

    3.3  Native Observation Encoding

    To supply physical observations to the 3D generator in a representation it natively understands, we bridge the estimated reference-view PBR maps T^2​D\widehat{T}_{\mathrm{2D}} directly to the surface of ℳ\mathcal{M} using the pretrained material encoder EmatE_{\mathrm{mat}}.

    Filtered surface projection. Through the camera projection π\pi, we associate each foreground pixel 𝐮\mathbf{u} of T^2​D\widehat{T}_{\mathrm{2D}} with its first visible surface hit 𝐩∈ℳ\mathbf{p}\in\mathcal{M}. At inference, foreground-mask erosion and local depth-discontinuity filtering further remove unreliable boundary correspondences. The retained correspondences form the observation set ℋvalid\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{valid}}, shared by all PBR channels. We voxelize the retained materials into a partial surface representation:

    𝒫o=Voxelize⁡({(𝐩,T^2​D​(𝐮))∣(𝐮,𝐩)∈ℋvalid}),\mathcal{P}_{o}=\operatorname{Voxelize}\!\left(\left\{\left(\mathbf{p},\widehat{T}_{\mathrm{2D}}(\mathbf{u})\right)\mid(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{p})\in\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{valid}}\right\}\right),(2)

    where 𝐮\mathbf{u} is a 2D pixel coordinate and 𝐩\mathbf{p} its surface location on ℳ\mathcal{M}; 𝒫o\mathcal{P}_{o} omits regions without valid observations.

    Sparse coordinate encoding. The partial surface attributes 𝒫o\mathcal{P}_{o} match the input domain of the pretrained material VAE, allowing direct ingestion by EmatE_{\mathrm{mat}} without intermediate adapters:

    Emat​(𝒫o)={(s,zso)∣s∈𝒮o},𝒮o⊆𝒮,E_{\mathrm{mat}}(\mathcal{P}_{o})=\left\{(s,z_{s}^{o})\mid s\in\mathcal{S}_{o}\right\},\qquad\mathcal{S}_{o}\subseteq\mathcal{S},(3)

    using the posterior mean. We call {zso}\{z_{s}^{o}\}native observation latents; 𝒮o\mathcal{S}_{o} indexes latent cells receiving observations.

    Zero-padding unobserved regions assigns concrete material values, such as black albedo, to surfaces without observations. We instead use the sparse coordinate architecture of EmatE_{\mathrm{mat}} to omit unobserved voxels. Encoding only the visible support 𝒫o\mathcal{P}_{o} avoids assigning explicit material values to unobserved voxels while retaining the visible support as conditioning evidence. This encoding runs once before sampling and remains fixed throughout generation. Section 4.4 examines how its latents and decoded materials differ from complete-material encoding.

    Spatial observation metadata. Each latent cell aggregates surface voxels, so an observed cell in 𝒮o\mathcal{S}_{o} is rarely fully covered from one view. The generator must quantify each cell’s observation support and proximity to unobserved regions. Let 𝒱s\mathcal{V}_{s} be the surface voxels in cell ss and 𝒱o\mathcal{V}_{o} the filtered, deduplicated set of observed voxels. Coverage is

    ρs=|𝒱s∩𝒱o||𝒱s|,s∈𝒮o,\rho_{s}=\frac{|\mathcal{V}_{s}\cap\mathcal{V}_{o}|}{|\mathcal{V}_{s}|},\qquad s\in\mathcal{S}_{o},(4)

    preventing repeated pixel projections onto one voxel from inflating coverage. Let 𝒰=𝒮∖𝒮o\mathcal{U}=\mathcal{S}\setminus\mathcal{S}_{o} be the unobserved cells and 𝒢𝒮\mathcal{G}_{\mathcal{S}} the six-neighbor graph over 𝒮\mathcal{S}; with 𝒰s⊆𝒰\mathcal{U}_{s}\subseteq\mathcal{U} the unobserved cells reachable from ss, the boundary distance is

    ds={minq∈𝒰s⁡dist𝒢𝒮⁡(s,q),𝒰s≠∅,−1,𝒰s=∅,d_{s}=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\min_{q\in\mathcal{U}_{s}}\operatorname{dist}_{\mathcal{G}_{\mathcal{S}}}(s,q),&\mathcal{U}_{s}\neq\varnothing,\\ -1,&\mathcal{U}_{s}=\varnothing,\end{cases}(5)

    measured in graph steps, with −1-1 marking cells from which no unobserved region is reachable. Both quantities describe the extent of observation, not the accuracy of the 2D estimate. These native observation latents and their spatial extent form the native observation representation

    𝒞o={(s,zso,ρs,ds)∣s∈𝒮o},\mathcal{C}_{o}=\left\{(s,z_{s}^{o},\rho_{s},d_{s})\mid s\in\mathcal{S}_{o}\right\},(6)

    which encapsulates native material observations alongside their physical extent without fictitious padding, ready to anchor full-surface generation. Because anchors are indexed in 3D coordinates, the same interface can combine observations from additional or edited views without retraining the generator (Appendix G.1).

    3.4  Observation-Guided Completion

    We generate complete material latents via flow matching over the mesh ℳ\mathcal{M}, predicting a velocity field at time tt from the current noisy material latents ZtZ_{t}, geometry latents GG, and native observation representation 𝒞o\mathcal{C}_{o}(Lipman et al., 2023). Native observation latents provide spatially aligned material evidence for reconstructing visible appearance. The generator must learn to use this evidence while completing unobserved surfaces coherently. Pixal3D⋆ injects projected image features through additive residuals and updates all surface tokens at every layer. We introduce an interleaved flow transformer that retains observations as fixed, read-only memory and alternates unobserved-cell and full-surface updates. This schedule assigns more hidden-state updates to unobserved cells while allowing visible materials to be refined during full-surface generation.

    Interleaved flow transformer. The generator uses two coordinate supports: the full active surface 𝒮\mathcal{S} and the observed subset 𝒮o⊆𝒮\mathcal{S}_{o}\subseteq\mathcal{S}. Figure 6 in Appendix A.2 illustrates the update schedule. We maintain two streams: a dynamic generation stream XX tracking the hidden state of ZtZ_{t} over 𝒮\mathcal{S}, and a static observation stream OO serving as immutable reference memory over 𝒮o\mathcal{S}_{o}. At observed coordinates, OsO_{s} stores partial evidence while XsX_{s} predicts the complete cell. Both streams use the same 3D coordinate frame and a shared input projection WinW_{\mathrm{in}} over material and geometry latents:

    Xs(0)\displaystyle X_{s}^{(0)}=Win​([Zt,s;gs]),\displaystyle=W_{\mathrm{in}}([Z_{t,s};g_{s}]),s∈𝒮,\displaystyle s\in\mathcal{S},(7)Os\displaystyle O_{s}=Win​([z¯so;gs])+Wmeta​([ρs;ds])+bo,\displaystyle=W_{\mathrm{in}}([\bar{z}_{s}^{o};g_{s}])+W_{\mathrm{meta}}([\rho_{s};d_{s}])+b_{o},s∈𝒮o,\displaystyle s\in\mathcal{S}_{o},

    where z¯so\bar{z}_{s}^{o} scales the native observation latents to match the normalization of ZtZ_{t}, WmetaW_{\mathrm{meta}} is a learnable affine projection of spatial metadata, and bob_{o} is a learned observation-role bias initialized to zero.

    Across the Transformer blocks, OO produces no queries and receives no updates with O(ℓ+1)=OO^{(\ell+1)}=O across blocks, serving as read-only memory supplying keys and values to every layer. To concentrate generative capacity on unobserved surfaces, query coordinates alternate across blocks ℓ=0,…,L−1\ell=0,\ldots,L-1: 𝒥ℓ=𝒰\mathcal{J}_{\ell}=\mathcal{U} for even ℓ\ell over unobserved cells 𝒰=𝒮∖𝒮o\mathcal{U}=\mathcal{S}\setminus\mathcal{S}_{o}, and 𝒥ℓ=𝒮\mathcal{J}_{\ell}=\mathcal{S} for odd ℓ\ell over the full surface to maintain global coherence. Let X~(ℓ)=Nℓ​(X(ℓ),t)\widetilde{X}^{(\ell)}=N_{\ell}(X^{(\ell)},t) and O~(ℓ)=Nℓ​(O,0)\widetilde{O}^{(\ell)}=N_{\ell}(O,0) denote the streams after normalization and time modulation, where observations carry a fixed clean-time indicator. The cross-stream attention is formulated as:

    Qℓ=qℓ(X~(ℓ)𝒥ℓ),Kℓ=[kℓ(O~(ℓ));kℓ(X~(ℓ))],Vℓ=[vℓ(O~(ℓ));vℓ(X~(ℓ))],\displaystyle Q_{\ell}=q_{\ell}\!\left(\widetilde{X}^{(\ell)}_{\mathcal{J}_{\ell}}\right),\quad K_{\ell}=\left[k_{\ell}\!\left(\widetilde{O}^{(\ell)}\right);k_{\ell}\!\left(\widetilde{X}^{(\ell)}\right)\right],\quad V_{\ell}=\left[v_{\ell}\!\left(\widetilde{O}^{(\ell)}\right);v_{\ell}\!\left(\widetilde{X}^{(\ell)}\right)\right],(8)Aℓ=softmax⁡(Qℓ​Kℓ⊤/dh)​Vℓ,\displaystyle A_{\ell}=\operatorname{softmax}\!\left(Q_{\ell}K_{\ell}^{\top}/\sqrt{d_{h}}\right)V_{\ell},

    where dh=128d_{h}=128 is the per-head dimension and qℓ,kℓq_{\ell},k_{\ell} apply 3D RoPE to latent coordinates, enabling attention based on relative position and content. Residual updates affect only 𝒥ℓ\mathcal{J}_{\ell}; other generation tokens are unchanged in that block, while OO remains fixed throughout. An output projection maps the terminal state X(L)X^{(L)} to predicted velocities for all of 𝒮\mathcal{S}. The full-surface training objective and sampling procedure are given in Sec. 3.5.

    3.5  Training and Inference

    Full-surface training objective. The generation stream XX synthesizes material latents over the surface 𝒮\mathcal{S}. Training observations are constructed from ground-truth materials of public 3D assets using visible-surface observation encoding, with complete material latents as targets. With ZgtZ_{\mathrm{gt}} the normalized ground-truth latents and ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,𝐈)\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}),

    Zt=(1−t)​Zgt+[σmin+(1−σmin)​t]​ϵ,v∗=(1−σmin)​ϵ−Zgt,Z_{t}=(1-t)Z_{\mathrm{gt}}+\left[\sigma_{\min}+(1-\sigma_{\min})t\right]\epsilon,\qquad v^{*}=(1-\sigma_{\min})\epsilon-Z_{\mathrm{gt}},(9)

    where σmin\sigma_{\min} is a small residual noise scale, t=1t=1 corresponds to pure noise, and t=0t=0 to material latents with residual noise σmin​ϵ\sigma_{\min}\epsilon. The loss is

    ℒFM=𝔼⁡[MSE⁡(vθ​(Zt,t,O,G),v∗)],\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\operatorname{MSE}\!\left(v_{\theta}(Z_{t},t;O,G),v^{*}\right)\right],(10)

    averaged over all valid tokens and channels, including observed coordinates. The observation representation remains fixed and is not noised along the flow path; it serves as conditioning input to the generator. The generation stream is supervised against complete-material targets over the entire surface, learning to reconstruct visible appearance from the fixed observations and to complete unobserved regions.

    Inference. Given dataset-provided or predicted geometry and cameras, we encode the mesh into GG and 𝒮\mathcal{S} and the filtered observations into anchors OO (Sec. 3.3). Starting from Z1∼𝒩⁡(0,𝐈)Z_{1}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbf{I}) over 𝒮\mathcal{S}, we integrate the learned velocity field with Euler steps, then de-normalize and decode the final latents with DmatD_{\mathrm{mat}} into full-surface PBR attributes for export. Optional KV caching reuses the observation stream’s per-layer keys and values across sampling steps; Table 6 reports its runtime and memory effects. Inference uses 25 Euler steps without classifier-free guidance on the time grid tj=3​uj/(1+2​uj)t_{j}=3u_{j}/(1+2u_{j}), uj=1−j/25u_{j}=1-j/25, j=0,…,25j=0,\ldots,25.

    4  Experiments

    The supplement covers datasets, implementation, baseline configurations, evaluation protocols, and additional analyses.

    Datasets. Our 3D material generator is trained solely on publicly available 3D datasets. The training sources are summarized in Appendix B.1. We evaluate on two datasets with no overlap with the training set: DTC-Tex, comprising 100 texture-rich product scans selected from the Digital Twin Catalog (Dong et al., 2025), and Complex-Tex, comprising 110 Sketchfab (Sketchfab, n.d.) meshes with denser inscriptions, finer patterns, and more varied shapes.

    Implementation details. The 2D material estimator adapts FireRed-Image-Edit-1.1 (Super Intelligence Team, 2026) at 1024×10241024\times 1024 resolution. The 3D generator uses 60 Transformer blocks, with self-attention initialized from TRELLIS.2 and the remaining components initialized randomly; the pretrained material encoder and decoder remain frozen. We train the generator with a global batch size of 576 using AdamW on 64 GPUs. Inference uses 25 Euler steps without classifier-free guidance.

    4.1  3D Generation with Given Geometry

    Setting and baselines. Each method textures the ground-truth mesh from a single forward-lit reference image. We record the ground-truth lighting and camera poses and render each textured result under these same conditions at the reference view and 15 novel views, isolating material quality from geometry, pose, and illumination differences. Table 1 compares ten baselines spanning native 3D generation and dedicated texturing methods. PBR methods are additionally evaluated on albedo, metallic, and roughness.

    Results. Table 1 shows that SUPRA-Tex leads across all shaded and PBR metrics on both datasets. Compared with feature-conditioned Pixal3D⋆, shaded PSNR improves by 1.7 dB and 1.2 dB, and albedo PSNRfg by 2.0 dB and 0.9 dB on DTC-Tex and Complex-Tex, respectively. The gains over multi-view PBR methods are larger: LumiTex trails by more than 2 dB in shaded PSNR and by over 1.5 dB in albedo PSNR on both datasets. The albedo gains and lowest metallic/roughness MAE show that the improvements extend to material attributes. Figure 2 shows that SUPRA-Tex better preserves the mug’s fine lettering and the plate’s intricate patterns than multi-view and feature-conditioned baselines, while novel-view renderings show coherent appearance on the completed surfaces.

    Table 2 separates the designated input view from the other 15 evaluation views, averaging novel-view scores per object before averaging over objects. For each method and metric, both splits use the same valid objects as Table 1. Novel views include both previously observed and unobserved surfaces; this split measures viewpoint generalization, rather than error exclusively on unseen surface regions.

    SUPRA-Tex achieves the best mean in every reported metric on both view splits and datasets. Against the strongest baseline for shaded PSNRfg in each split, reference-view gains are 2.562.56 dB on DTC-Tex and 0.950.95 dB on Complex-Tex (TEXGen), while novel-view gains are 1.761.76 and 1.091.09 dB (Pixal3D⋆). The split supports improved reference-view fidelity together with improved novel-view appearance.

    4.2  End-to-End Single-Image-to-3D Generation

    Setting and baselines. Each method generates both geometry and appearance end-to-end from a single reference image, without access to ground-truth geometry or cameras during generation.

    We compare with TRELLIS.2, Pixal3D⋆, Hunyuan3D 2.1, Step1X-3D, UniLat3D, and CUPID ; ; ; ; ; (Xiang et al., 2026Li et al., 2026aTencent Hunyuan3D Team, 2025bLi et al., 2025aWu et al., 2026aHuang et al., 2026). SUPRA-Tex and Pixal3D⋆ share geometry predicted by the latter, with separate appearance pipelines. Other baselines generate their own geometry. For scoring, outputs are brought into a common coordinate frame, with GT similarity alignment applied to methods marked †\dagger in Table 3; this alignment plays no role in generation.

    Results. Table 3 shows that SUPRA-Tex leads across all 99 metrics on both datasets. Relative to Pixal3D⋆, four-view PSNR improves by 1.77 dB on DTC-Tex and 2.49 dB on Complex-Tex, foreground PSNR by 0.89 dB and 1.60 dB, and LPIPS decreases by 64.8% and 58.6%, respectively. Higher reference-view CLIP-I and lower 16-view distribution distances further indicate stronger input consistency and multi-view appearance quality. Since Pixal3D⋆ and SUPRA-Tex share predicted geometry, these results show that our appearance pipeline retains its advantage on predicted surfaces, complementing the given-geometry results in Table 1.

    4.3  Commercial Comparisons

    We evaluate SUPRA-Tex against five commercial systems on 45 real and synthetic images. We use two-view conditioning only for commercial comparisons, combining the reference image with a back view synthesized from it.

    Without ground-truth geometry or cameras, paired human preferences and VLM ratings assess input alignment, PBR plausibility, and visual quality. Trained solely on public data, SUPRA-Tex receives 51.1%–84.8% preference in human visual-quality comparisons and ties for the highest VLM PBR score of 8.67 (Table 5). Figure 3 illustrates reference-detail preservation and coherent surface completion.

    4.4  Ablation and Analysis

    We evaluate the observation-injection architecture and material content under the given-geometry protocol of Sec. 4.1. The architecture variants share training data, initialization protocol, optimization settings, training budget, and checkpoint-selection rule. All comparisons use the same geometry, cameras, valid observation support, and sampling seed.

    How observations are used. Table 5 compares three conditioning designs with the same predicted PBR observations. Residual injection adds encoded observations through layerwise residuals. Joint-update attention updates observation states in selected layers and all generation states in every layer. In contrast, SUPRA-Tex keeps observations read-only and alternates unobserved-cell and full-surface updates (Sec. 3.4). It improves shaded PSNRfg over residual injection by 0.87 dB on DTC-Tex and 0.29 dB on Complex-Tex, and matches joint-update attention in shaded fidelity while improving albedo PSNRfg by 0.15 and 0.16 dB with lower MR MAE. Thus, the design preserves or improves reconstruction quality without spending computation on observation-state updates or full-surface queries at every block. The complete design also samples 1.20×1.20\times and 1.18×1.18\times faster than joint-update attention on the two datasets (Sec. 4.5).

item.title: Stable Signer V3: 4D Deformable Primitive Splatting Is All You Need for Sign Language Production

Stable Signer V3: 4D Deformable Primitive Splatting Is All You Need for Sign Language Production

Sen Fang Liwei Che Dimitris N. Metaxas Rutgers University Affiliation: Affiliation: https://signerx.github.io/Stable-Signer-V3

Abstract

We present , an interactive high-resolution sign language avatar system built on . It addresses three limitations of existing avatars: restricted facial expression, inaccurate identity-specific body deformation, and loss of fine appearance details. adds transferable superquadric primitives for richer expression control; learns an identity-specific virtual muscle layer for more faithful motion; and uses TunnelingNet to recover identity-specific high-resolution details. Both test-time modules are optimized once per signer identity; inference then runs entirely from the stored identity parameters. Together, they reduce facial geometry error by 71.4%, body-boundary error by 35.1% across ten identities, and high-resolution RGB reconstruction error by 24.2% on held-out evaluations, while retaining interactive streaming.Stable Signer V34D Deformable Primitive SplattingShared Face Primitive SplattingTest-Time Body Primitive SplattingTest-Time Tunneling Super-Resolution

1

Sign language production aims to translate text or lexical sequences into intelligible, natural, and expressive signing videos . Sign language conveys information through coordinated manual gestures, facial expressions, head poses, and body movements . A practical production system must therefore go beyond predicting skeletons or parametric poses: it must consistently express these motions through avatars with diverse identities and appearances, preserve subtle expressions and visual details, and meet the latency requirements of interactive applications .[, , ]57497[, , , ]4325178[, , ]261661

Existing approaches broadly follow two routes. synthesizes signing videos from intermediate poses with pose-conditioned image or video generation models . predicts language-conditioned 3D signing motion and uses it to animate explicit characters . Pose-guided human-video models provide additional tools for this pipeline . Dictionary-based production also exploits reusable signing segments and their transitions . Pose generation models provide structured representations of signing motion . Within these pipelines, 3D Gaussian splatting  enables efficient rendering, with recent extensions supporting signing avatars  and real-time upper-body animation . Fine-grained signing remains a central rendering challenge even with accurate 3D pose prediction and fast rendering. The resulting motion is jointly constrained by the local expressiveness of the parametric human model, the compatibility between template deformation and individual geometry, and the image decoder’s ability to reconstruct fine details. We investigate how compact adaptation mechanisms can improve signing expression by building on existing motion and avatar priors.Text2Pose2Video[, , , , , , ]5758485054638Text2Avatar[, , , , , ]18634132077[, , , ]935845[, ]6362[, , , , ]495170737[]25[, ]1320[]77

Three challenges motivate this work. First, the compact expression spaces of parametric face models such as FLAME  suppress subtle local motion and impose a geometric ceiling on facial detail. Second, shared skinning and deformation rules cannot consistently accommodate identity-specific body shape and local surface motion . An avatar that appears plausible in its reference pose can therefore develop local shape errors as the pose changes. Third, general-purpose decoders can discard identity-specific high-frequency details when reconstructing images from compact Gaussian features . These challenges concern facial control, identity-specific body deformation, and high-resolution appearance, respectively. Together, they limit the quality of existing sign language production systems.[]30[, , , ]28851538[, , ]712477

To address these challenges, we introduce , a sign language production system based on . Our key idea is to introduce a learnable local deformation layer between the parametric human model and the avatar, separating shared facial motion capabilities from identity-specific body and appearance adaptation. We instantiate the deformable primitives as superquadrics, allowing local residual deformations to vary with pose and expression while preserving the existing human control interface and avatar bindings. Given text or gloss input, the system uses SignSparK  for motion completion and GUAVA  for avatar initialization and feature rendering. A shared facial layer learns local residual deformations driven by FLAME expression, jaw, and eye controls and transfers them to the avatar through surface bindings. For the body, a pose-conditioned virtual muscle layer is fitted to each identity from reference videos; it corrects geometry before skinning so that bound Gaussians follow the adjusted surface, with displacement and smoothness constraints discouraging implausible deformations. For appearance, an independently normalized Softmax tunneling path uses terminal decoder semantics to learn identity-specific high-resolution detail while preserving the early Gaussian feature pathway. Test-time adaptation forms a one-time per-identity character-preparation stage. The resulting body and detail parameters serve every subsequent sequence, cleanly separating identity adaptation from online generation.Stable Signer V34D Deformable Primitive Splatting[]34[]77

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    A shared deformable primitive layer enables more complex and controllable facial expressions.Shared Face Primitive Splatting.

  • •

    An identity-specific virtual muscle layer adapts body deformation from reference videos while keeping the avatar generation backbone frozen.Test-Time Body Primitive Splatting.

  • •

    A late tunneling path learns identity-specific high-resolution detail from reference videos and stores it in the deployed decoder.Test-Time Tunneling Super-Resolution.

    • 2

    Resources such as WLASL , How2Sign , JWSign , and YouTube-SL-25  support research across lexical signs, continuous signing, and multiple languages. Pose-conditioned video synthesis has been explored through Text2Sign , SignSynth , and Everybody Sign Now , with subsequent work on appearance control, large-scale co-articulation, and diffusion-based synthesis . Broader human-video synthesis develops pose-guided generation through DreaMoving , Follow Your Pose , and MimicMotion , with ControlVideo  and Wan-Animate  further exploring controllable video generation and character animation. The 3D route combines signing-motion generation  with controllable avatar rendering . For motion generation, some methods retrieve and concatenate signing clips from existing dictionaries , while others learn to predict continuous motion from language inputs using progressive prediction or motion primitives . Motion modeling has also explored adversarial training, skeletal graph structure, and non-autoregressive generation . Related text-to-human-motion research studies diffusion-based synthesis and language-like motion modeling , providing a broader context for language-conditioned animation. Recent motion generators explore discrete diffusion for gloss-to-pose synthesis , autoregressive motion tokens , and multilingual generation from text and prompts . SignSparK  combines sparse keyframe control with conditional flow matching to generate dense 3D signing motion. Appearance transfer in skeletal pose sequences further studies how signer-specific characteristics can be changed while retaining signing motion . Together, these directions address motion accuracy, co-articulation, appearance control, and efficient generation . We build on this motion completion capability and focus on facial, body, and appearance adaptation for personalized avatar rendering.Sign Language Production.[]29[]6[]10[]59[]57[]58[]48[, , ]50548[]9[]35[]84[]83[]5[, , ]18634[, , ]132077[, , , ]76546362[, , ]495152[, , ]475317[, , ]806021[]70[]73[]7[]34[]37[, ]1661

    SMPL-X  provides joint body, hand, and facial controls for animatable humans, while FLAME  models facial shape, expression, and articulation. These parametric representations support pose-driven signing avatars . Whole-body reconstruction methods, including SMPLer-X and component-aware mesh recovery , and dedicated hand reconstruction  support detailed avatar controls; DWPose provides complementary whole-body keypoint estimates . Complementary work improves 3D pose estimation for sign language  and resolves hand-to-hand intersections , supporting more reliable motion inputs. Accurate facial and body motion is particularly relevant to signing, where non-manual cues contribute to meaning . Building on 3D Gaussian splatting , SplattingAvatar  embeds Gaussians on a deformable mesh surface, while GART  learns forward skinning and latent bones to capture articulated and non-rigid motion. Articulated Gaussian models further explore cage-based deformation in D3GA , monocular human reconstruction in GauHuman , and efficient human rendering in ASH and HiFi4G . Related efforts address monocular Gaussian avatar reconstruction in GVA , image-based body estimation in GST , and generalizable sparse-view synthesis in GHG . Expressive avatar reconstruction is also studied by X-Avatar  and EVA , with EVA learning Gaussian human avatars from monocular RGB video. SignSplat  adapts Gaussian avatars to signing through sequence-level mesh fitting and Gaussian regularization, emphasizing accurate hands and facial expressions. We retain structured human controls and surface bindings while adding a shared facial residual layer and identity-specific body deformation.3D Humans and Gaussian Avatars for Sign Language.[]40[]30[, ]186[, ]332[]41[]72[]18[]19[, ]2678[]25[]55[]28[]85[]15[, ]3824[]33[]44[]27[]56[]13[]20

    Video-based character reconstruction has developed through HumanNeRF  and NeuMan , with Vid2Avatar exploring self-supervised scene decomposition for videos in the wild . Efficient character preparation is explored by InstantAvatar , which learns avatars from monocular video. Subject-specific optimization can recover detailed avatar appearance: Gaussian Head Avatar  jointly learns neutral Gaussians and an expression-driven deformation field for high-fidelity 2K head rendering. Reference-conditioned image and video synthesis transfers appearance from exemplar images . High-resolution conditional synthesis and latent diffusion provide complementary image-generation frameworks , with ControlNet  and ControlNeXt  exploring additional conditioning for image and video generation. For 3D avatars, GUAVA  predicts an animatable upper-body Gaussian avatar from a single image and refines rendered features with a neural decoder. Lightweight adaptation offers a way to reuse pretrained representations: LoRA  learns low-rank weight updates, and LLaMA-Adapter  introduces new conditioning through zero-initialized attention. Adapters also connect pretrained visual representations to dense prediction tasks . These adaptation mechanisms motivate compact trainable paths around a frozen backbone. We combine generalizable avatar initialization with identity-specific adaptation of body geometry and high-resolution appearance. Character reference videos supervise a body deformation layer and a detail module at the decoder’s terminal stage, with the pretrained backbone held fixed. Both modules are optimized once per signer, and online signing directly reuses the stored parameters.Personalized Avatars and Test-Time Training.[]69[]23[]11[]22[]71[, ]7564[, ]6546[]79[]42[]77[]12[]81[]4

    3

    3.1

    Given text or gloss input, SignSparK  completes dictionary-retrieved sparse poses into body, hand, and facial controls . GUAVA  initializes a surface-bound Gaussian avatar from a reference image. We augment this pipeline with shared facial deformation and identity-specific body and appearance adaptation.[]34{𝐪t}t=1T\{\mathbf{q}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}[]77

Motion synthesis and primitive deformation run at 198.7 and 320.9 FPS, while HD avatar rendering and 4K detail refinement reach 52.0 and 47.6 FPS. A warmed 784-frame, three-chunk text-to-HD-avatar run completes in 31.0 seconds wall time (25.3 generated FPS), including composition, motion synthesis, streamed rendering, encoding, and chunk concatenation. We re-extract signing poses from each rendered video and translate them with the same frozen back-translation model. Activating all three components raises BLEU-4 from 25.6450 to 26.8897 (4.9%) and ROUGE-L from 59.4771 to 61.7298 (3.8%). The complete enhancement stack therefore improves geometric and rendering fidelity while fully preserving the underlying signs.Back-translation evaluation.4

    Table  first compares our system with four reproducible open-source avatar methods at one shared held-out pose for each of four input reference videos. We compute PSNR inside the shared ground-truth foreground mask and SSIM/LPIPS within the same ground-truth person bounding box, then macro-average identities. The second block evaluates our identity-adapted renderer against frozen GUAVA using matched cached features and crops sampled directly from held-out 4K targets.Rendering fidelity.5

    The second block measures identity adaptation by comparing frozen GUAVA and our complete renderer on the same held-out subset from each of ten reference videos. Both methods receive identical cached Gaussian features, crop coordinates, and crops sampled directly from the held-out 4K frames. Macro-averaged over identities, Stable Signer V3 raises PSNR from 19.418 to 21.790 dB and SSIM from 0.833 to 0.860, while reducing LPIPS from 0.245 to 0.226. This corresponds to a 2.372 dB PSNR gain and an 8.0% relative LPIPS reduction over the frozen renderer.768×768768{\times}768

    4.6

    Figure  compares methods column by column on the same sign-language sequence. The four published baselines are followed by our method and Ground Truth. The shared framing makes facial detail, finger articulation, and garment boundaries directly comparable across columns. Across identities and poses, our method preserves facial character, articulated fingers, silhouettes, and garment boundaries more consistently than the reproduced baselines.7

    5

    We presented Stable Signer V3, a sign language production framework combining shared facial primitives, test-time identity-specific body primitives, and a tunneling decoder for high-resolution appearance. Together, they unify expressive control and personalized rendering through a reusable deformable representation. Reference-video adaptation is performed once, after which the stored identity parameters drive subsequent signing sequences. On held-out evaluations, the three modules reduce head reconstruction error by 71.4%, body-boundary error by 35.1% across ten identities, and high-resolution RGB reconstruction error by 24.2%, while retaining interactive inference. Future work will broaden signer and motion coverage and include evaluation by proficient sign-language users.

Stable Signer V3: 4D Deformable Primitive Splatting Is All You Need for Sign Language Production

Sen Fang Liwei Che Dimitris N. Metaxas Rutgers University Affiliation: Affiliation: https://signerx.github.io/Stable-Signer-V3

Abstract

We present , an interactive high-resolution sign language avatar system built on . It addresses three limitations of existing avatars: restricted facial expression, inaccurate identity-specific body deformation, and loss of fine appearance details. adds transferable superquadric primitives for richer expression control; learns an identity-specific virtual muscle layer for more faithful motion; and uses TunnelingNet to recover identity-specific high-resolution details. Both test-time modules are optimized once per signer identity; inference then runs entirely from the stored identity parameters. Together, they reduce facial geometry error by 71.4%, body-boundary error by 35.1% across ten identities, and high-resolution RGB reconstruction error by 24.2% on held-out evaluations, while retaining interactive streaming.Stable Signer V34D Deformable Primitive SplattingShared Face Primitive SplattingTest-Time Body Primitive SplattingTest-Time Tunneling Super-Resolution

1

Sign language production aims to translate text or lexical sequences into intelligible, natural, and expressive signing videos . Sign language conveys information through coordinated manual gestures, facial expressions, head poses, and body movements . A practical production system must therefore go beyond predicting skeletons or parametric poses: it must consistently express these motions through avatars with diverse identities and appearances, preserve subtle expressions and visual details, and meet the latency requirements of interactive applications .[, , ]57497[, , , ]4325178[, , ]261661

Existing approaches broadly follow two routes. synthesizes signing videos from intermediate poses with pose-conditioned image or video generation models . predicts language-conditioned 3D signing motion and uses it to animate explicit characters . Pose-guided human-video models provide additional tools for this pipeline . Dictionary-based production also exploits reusable signing segments and their transitions . Pose generation models provide structured representations of signing motion . Within these pipelines, 3D Gaussian splatting  enables efficient rendering, with recent extensions supporting signing avatars  and real-time upper-body animation . Fine-grained signing remains a central rendering challenge even with accurate 3D pose prediction and fast rendering. The resulting motion is jointly constrained by the local expressiveness of the parametric human model, the compatibility between template deformation and individual geometry, and the image decoder’s ability to reconstruct fine details. We investigate how compact adaptation mechanisms can improve signing expression by building on existing motion and avatar priors.Text2Pose2Video[, , , , , , ]5758485054638Text2Avatar[, , , , , ]18634132077[, , , ]935845[, ]6362[, , , , ]495170737[]25[, ]1320[]77

Three challenges motivate this work. First, the compact expression spaces of parametric face models such as FLAME  suppress subtle local motion and impose a geometric ceiling on facial detail. Second, shared skinning and deformation rules cannot consistently accommodate identity-specific body shape and local surface motion . An avatar that appears plausible in its reference pose can therefore develop local shape errors as the pose changes. Third, general-purpose decoders can discard identity-specific high-frequency details when reconstructing images from compact Gaussian features . These challenges concern facial control, identity-specific body deformation, and high-resolution appearance, respectively. Together, they limit the quality of existing sign language production systems.[]30[, , , ]28851538[, , ]712477

To address these challenges, we introduce , a sign language production system based on . Our key idea is to introduce a learnable local deformation layer between the parametric human model and the avatar, separating shared facial motion capabilities from identity-specific body and appearance adaptation. We instantiate the deformable primitives as superquadrics, allowing local residual deformations to vary with pose and expression while preserving the existing human control interface and avatar bindings. Given text or gloss input, the system uses SignSparK  for motion completion and GUAVA  for avatar initialization and feature rendering. A shared facial layer learns local residual deformations driven by FLAME expression, jaw, and eye controls and transfers them to the avatar through surface bindings. For the body, a pose-conditioned virtual muscle layer is fitted to each identity from reference videos; it corrects geometry before skinning so that bound Gaussians follow the adjusted surface, with displacement and smoothness constraints discouraging implausible deformations. For appearance, an independently normalized Softmax tunneling path uses terminal decoder semantics to learn identity-specific high-resolution detail while preserving the early Gaussian feature pathway. Test-time adaptation forms a one-time per-identity character-preparation stage. The resulting body and detail parameters serve every subsequent sequence, cleanly separating identity adaptation from online generation.Stable Signer V34D Deformable Primitive Splatting[]34[]77

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    A shared deformable primitive layer enables more complex and controllable facial expressions.Shared Face Primitive Splatting.

  • •

    An identity-specific virtual muscle layer adapts body deformation from reference videos while keeping the avatar generation backbone frozen.Test-Time Body Primitive Splatting.

  • •

    A late tunneling path learns identity-specific high-resolution detail from reference videos and stores it in the deployed decoder.Test-Time Tunneling Super-Resolution.

    • 2

    Resources such as WLASL , How2Sign , JWSign , and YouTube-SL-25  support research across lexical signs, continuous signing, and multiple languages. Pose-conditioned video synthesis has been explored through Text2Sign , SignSynth , and Everybody Sign Now , with subsequent work on appearance control, large-scale co-articulation, and diffusion-based synthesis . Broader human-video synthesis develops pose-guided generation through DreaMoving , Follow Your Pose , and MimicMotion , with ControlVideo  and Wan-Animate  further exploring controllable video generation and character animation. The 3D route combines signing-motion generation  with controllable avatar rendering . For motion generation, some methods retrieve and concatenate signing clips from existing dictionaries , while others learn to predict continuous motion from language inputs using progressive prediction or motion primitives . Motion modeling has also explored adversarial training, skeletal graph structure, and non-autoregressive generation . Related text-to-human-motion research studies diffusion-based synthesis and language-like motion modeling , providing a broader context for language-conditioned animation. Recent motion generators explore discrete diffusion for gloss-to-pose synthesis , autoregressive motion tokens , and multilingual generation from text and prompts . SignSparK  combines sparse keyframe control with conditional flow matching to generate dense 3D signing motion. Appearance transfer in skeletal pose sequences further studies how signer-specific characteristics can be changed while retaining signing motion . Together, these directions address motion accuracy, co-articulation, appearance control, and efficient generation . We build on this motion completion capability and focus on facial, body, and appearance adaptation for personalized avatar rendering.Sign Language Production.[]29[]6[]10[]59[]57[]58[]48[, , ]50548[]9[]35[]84[]83[]5[, , ]18634[, , ]132077[, , , ]76546362[, , ]495152[, , ]475317[, , ]806021[]70[]73[]7[]34[]37[, ]1661

    SMPL-X  provides joint body, hand, and facial controls for animatable humans, while FLAME  models facial shape, expression, and articulation. These parametric representations support pose-driven signing avatars . Whole-body reconstruction methods, including SMPLer-X and component-aware mesh recovery , and dedicated hand reconstruction  support detailed avatar controls; DWPose provides complementary whole-body keypoint estimates . Complementary work improves 3D pose estimation for sign language  and resolves hand-to-hand intersections , supporting more reliable motion inputs. Accurate facial and body motion is particularly relevant to signing, where non-manual cues contribute to meaning . Building on 3D Gaussian splatting , SplattingAvatar  embeds Gaussians on a deformable mesh surface, while GART  learns forward skinning and latent bones to capture articulated and non-rigid motion. Articulated Gaussian models further explore cage-based deformation in D3GA , monocular human reconstruction in GauHuman , and efficient human rendering in ASH and HiFi4G . Related efforts address monocular Gaussian avatar reconstruction in GVA , image-based body estimation in GST , and generalizable sparse-view synthesis in GHG . Expressive avatar reconstruction is also studied by X-Avatar  and EVA , with EVA learning Gaussian human avatars from monocular RGB video. SignSplat  adapts Gaussian avatars to signing through sequence-level mesh fitting and Gaussian regularization, emphasizing accurate hands and facial expressions. We retain structured human controls and surface bindings while adding a shared facial residual layer and identity-specific body deformation.3D Humans and Gaussian Avatars for Sign Language.[]40[]30[, ]186[, ]332[]41[]72[]18[]19[, ]2678[]25[]55[]28[]85[]15[, ]3824[]33[]44[]27[]56[]13[]20

    Video-based character reconstruction has developed through HumanNeRF  and NeuMan , with Vid2Avatar exploring self-supervised scene decomposition for videos in the wild . Efficient character preparation is explored by InstantAvatar , which learns avatars from monocular video. Subject-specific optimization can recover detailed avatar appearance: Gaussian Head Avatar  jointly learns neutral Gaussians and an expression-driven deformation field for high-fidelity 2K head rendering. Reference-conditioned image and video synthesis transfers appearance from exemplar images . High-resolution conditional synthesis and latent diffusion provide complementary image-generation frameworks , with ControlNet  and ControlNeXt  exploring additional conditioning for image and video generation. For 3D avatars, GUAVA  predicts an animatable upper-body Gaussian avatar from a single image and refines rendered features with a neural decoder. Lightweight adaptation offers a way to reuse pretrained representations: LoRA  learns low-rank weight updates, and LLaMA-Adapter  introduces new conditioning through zero-initialized attention. Adapters also connect pretrained visual representations to dense prediction tasks . These adaptation mechanisms motivate compact trainable paths around a frozen backbone. We combine generalizable avatar initialization with identity-specific adaptation of body geometry and high-resolution appearance. Character reference videos supervise a body deformation layer and a detail module at the decoder’s terminal stage, with the pretrained backbone held fixed. Both modules are optimized once per signer, and online signing directly reuses the stored parameters.Personalized Avatars and Test-Time Training.[]69[]23[]11[]22[]71[, ]7564[, ]6546[]79[]42[]77[]12[]81[]4

    3

    3.1

    Given text or gloss input, SignSparK  completes dictionary-retrieved sparse poses into body, hand, and facial controls . GUAVA  initializes a surface-bound Gaussian avatar from a reference image. We augment this pipeline with shared facial deformation and identity-specific body and appearance adaptation.[]34{𝐪t}t=1T\{\mathbf{q}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}[]77

    We learn appearance parameters from aligned video frames with fixed geometry and Gaussian features. The native-resolution head receives RGB, gradient, high-pass, and local-detail supervision:

    Here is the intermediate loss above; and are nonnegative weights. The crop is shared by prediction and target, and indexes the native-resolution loss terms.     4

    4.1

    The evaluation covers facial expression reconstruction, identity-specific body adaptation, and high-resolution detail recovery.

    Controlled face and body studies use chronological 80%/20% training–evaluation splits and fixed optimization budgets; checkpoint selection uses the training segment exclusively. Detail adaptation is evaluated on held-out frames, and cross-method rendering uses identical poses, cameras, backgrounds, and target-defined crops for every method. Scores are first aggregated per identity and then macro-averaged.Data and protocol.

    Facial geometry is measured by Euclidean point error in the native shared tracked coordinates. Body adaptation reports refined RGB L1, boundary L1, and SSIM . Rendering comparisons use foreground PSNR  together with SSIM and LPIPS  inside a shared ground-truth person crop. Runtime measurements distinguish independently warmed stage throughput from measured resident-pipeline wall time. Semantic preservation is evaluated through fixed back-translation using BLEU-4  and ROUGE-L F1  on poses re-extracted from the rendered RGB videos.Metrics.[]67[]68[]82[]39[]31

    4.2

    We train the shared face layer on the tracked FLAME sequence provided with GUAVA , using a chronological 80%/20% training–evaluation split and a fixed optimization budget. The restricted FLAME carrier and the full-expression target share identical articulation, isolating the expression geometry that our layer must recover.[]77

    Table  reports Euclidean error over all retained head samples, including template- and UV-bound samples: mean head error falls from 1.267 to 0.362 mm (71.4%), and facial error falls from 1.492 to 0.518 mm. Figure  shows the held-out midpoint with a shared error scale and deviation magnification. The shared primitive controller reduces head error by 71.4% and recovers fine expression geometry across the face; region-wise results are provided in the supplement.145×5\times

    4.3

    Figure  compares frozen GUAVA, an Adapter, and our tunneling decoder through synchronized facial crops. The 512-resolution baseline is enlarged for display. Both adapted outputs are generated at 1024 resolution, and the visualization presents the combined effect of adaptation and native-resolution decoding. All trainable variants use the same frames, Gaussian features, targets, optimizer, and update budget. On held-out frames, Adapter reduces mean RGB L1 by 13.5%, while tunneling reduces it by 24.2% relative to the frozen baseline.6

    4.4

    Under a fixed 249-step adaptation budget and chronological 80%/20% training–evaluation split, Table  shows that increasing from 512 to 1,024 reduces refined RGB L1 from 0.0599 to 0.0575 and boundary L1 from 0.0282 to 0.0270.2KK

    Figure  compares frozen GUAVA with identity-specific Body SQ under the same frame, pose, and camera; the learned layer locally adapts the carrier around the torso and upper arms.5

    Reference overlays locate the learned patches, carrier views expose their geometric support, and RGB errors use the same range with darker colors indicating larger error, separating surface alignment from its effect on rendering. Figure  highlights the resulting geometric fit, and Table  confirms simultaneous gains in RGB fidelity, boundary alignment, and structural similarity.[0,0.08][0,0.08]52

    4.5

    Table  reports warmed batch-one component throughput on a single Quadro RTX 8000. Motion synthesis and primitive deformation run at 198.7 and 320.9 FPS, while HD avatar rendering and 4K detail refinement reach 52.0 and 47.6 FPS. In the resident pipeline, stages overlap across streaming chunks. A warmed 784-frame, three-chunk text-to-HD-avatar run completes in 31.0 seconds wall time (25.3 generated FPS), including composition, motion synthesis, streamed rendering, encoding, and chunk concatenation. Body and detail adaptation are performed once for each new avatar and baked into the deployed model; subsequent sequences run directly from the baked parameters.Online efficiency.3

    Table  tests whether the proposed visual enhancement components alter the linguistic content of the output. Both configurations render the same motion sequence; the full configuration additionally activates shared face primitives, test-time body primitives, and detail tunneling. We re-extract signing poses from each rendered video and translate them with the same frozen back-translation model. Activating all three components raises BLEU-4 from 25.6450 to 26.8897 (4.9%) and ROUGE-L from 59.4771 to 61.7298 (3.8%). The complete enhancement stack therefore improves geometric and rendering fidelity while fully preserving the underlying signs.Back-translation evaluation.4

    Table  first compares our system with four reproducible open-source avatar methods at one shared held-out pose for each of four input reference videos. We compute PSNR inside the shared ground-truth foreground mask and SSIM/LPIPS within the same ground-truth person bounding box, then macro-average identities. The second block evaluates our identity-adapted renderer against frozen GUAVA using matched cached features and crops sampled directly from held-out 4K targets.Rendering fidelity.5

    The second block measures identity adaptation by comparing frozen GUAVA and our complete renderer on the same held-out subset from each of ten reference videos. Both methods receive identical cached Gaussian features, crop coordinates, and crops sampled directly from the held-out 4K frames. Macro-averaged over identities, Stable Signer V3 raises PSNR from 19.418 to 21.790 dB and SSIM from 0.833 to 0.860, while reducing LPIPS from 0.245 to 0.226. This corresponds to a 2.372 dB PSNR gain and an 8.0% relative LPIPS reduction over the frozen renderer.768×768768{\times}768

    4.6

    Figure  compares methods column by column on the same sign-language sequence. The four published baselines are followed by our method and Ground Truth. The shared framing makes facial detail, finger articulation, and garment boundaries directly comparable across columns. Across identities and poses, our method preserves facial character, articulated fingers, silhouettes, and garment boundaries more consistently than the reproduced baselines.7

    5

    We presented Stable Signer V3, a sign language production framework combining shared facial primitives, test-time identity-specific body primitives, and a tunneling decoder for high-resolution appearance. Together, they unify expressive control and personalized rendering through a reusable deformable representation. Reference-video adaptation is performed once, after which the stored identity parameters drive subsequent signing sequences. On held-out evaluations, the three modules reduce head reconstruction error by 71.4%, body-boundary error by 35.1% across ten identities, and high-resolution RGB reconstruction error by 24.2%, while retaining interactive inference. Future work will broaden signer and motion coverage and include evaluation by proficient sign-language users.

item.title: 清华特奖得主AI创业再+1：GeoPT一作入局物理世界模型
item.description:
来源：量子位（中文） 相关度：13.5 正文：1982 字 / 7 图

命中：世界模型

从搭载物理建模能力的世界模型切入

< img id="wx_img" src="https://www.qbitai.com/wp-content/uploads/imgs/qbitai-logo-1.png" width="400" height="400">

清华特奖得主AI创业再+1：GeoPT一作入局物理世界模型

梦晨2026-10-1620:54:54 来源：量子位

从搭载物理建模能力的世界模型切入

衡宇 发自 凹非寺 量子位 | 公众号QbitAI

世界模型赛道仍在源源不断涌入最智慧的大脑。

量子位获悉，。曾在2022年获清华特奖的吴海旭，已于今年悄然开启世界模型创业

公司名为物原科技，迄今为止迅速完成了多轮融资，公司估值来到数亿美元，投资方队伍中出现了蚂蚁、美团、达晨财智、星连等一线投资机构的的身影。

今年2月，在技术领域引起热议。吴海旭为一作的工作GeoPT

该工作提出了一种全新的动力学提升预训练范式，通过合成动力学（Synthetic Dynamics）将静态几何“提升”到动态空间，让模型在无标签数据上通过学习粒子轨迹演化来获取物理直觉。

该论文的作者中还出现了清华软件学院长聘副教授（吴海旭博士导师）、MIT，以及MIT教授（吴海旭博士后所在项目组导师）等人。龙明盛何恺明Wojciech Matusik

我们获悉，吴海旭此次创业，选择从切入。搭载物理建模能力的世界模型

据接近物原科技的知情人士透露，该方案一定程度上在技术思路方面延续了GeoPT的研究路线。

吴海旭是谁？

吴海旭于2016年进入清华大学软件学院软件工程专业就读本科，并于次年起在清华数学科学系纯数学与应用数学攻读第二学位。

2019年暑期，他曾作为访问学生进入哈佛大学Visual Computing Group开展研究，导师为教授Hanspeter Pfister。

本科毕业后，他在清华大学软件学院开始了自己的研究生生涯，导师为副教授龙明盛。

龙明盛课题组早期研究迁移学习（Transfer Learning），后来重点转向时序基础模型、时空预测、AI for Science、多模态世界模型等等。

2022年，吴海旭获得了清华的特等奖学金。

清华特奖的含金量大家应该多少有所耳闻，月之暗面杨植麟、OpenAI陈立杰、谷歌姚顺宇（江湖传言其已离职，创业RSI）、Sand.ai曹越、LiberAI刘松铭等都曾获得该奖项。

特奖答辩时，吴海旭就已经在ICML、NeurIPS、IEEE TPAMI等CCF-A类会议/期刊上发表论文7篇，其中一作/共一6篇。

，该工作首次系统性地将序列分解思想与改进的注意力机制深度融合，被称为长时序预测（LSTF）里程碑模型。当时他的核心研究成果是Autoformer

Autoformer后，他又发表了PredRNN、 Corrformer、Transolver、GeoPT等工作。

2025年起，他，GeoPT正是这一时期他的代表性工作。前往MIT CSAIL从事博士后工作

这期间，吴海旭的博士后导师Wojciech Matusik是计算设计与制造领域的知名学者。他的研究横跨计算机图形学、计算制造、机器人学等多个方向，致力于用算法连接数字世界与物理制造。

吴海旭现在的个人主页上注明，其个人的。研究重点主要面向深度学习与科学机器学习，目标是为物理系统构建可扩展原则

其研究聚焦物理系统与动力系统两大主题，主要分为以下三个方向：

基于物理原理的可扩展骨干网络（Autoformer、Corrformer、Transolver）

端到端物理基础模型（TimesNet、Unisolver、GeoPT）

领域感知型科学学习系统（Flowformer、Transolver++、FlashBias）

截至目前，吴海旭的。谷歌学术被引用数为29611

参考链接：[1]https://wuhaixu2016.github.io/[2]https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=oLL_x0wAAAAJ&hl=en[3]https://people.csail.mit.edu/wojciech/[4]https://www.thss.tsinghua.edu.cn/info/1023/2032.htm

item.title: Walk in Envelopes: Efficient Branching Walk-on-Spheres via Certified Solution Bounds
item.description:
来源：arXiv·cs.GR 最新（English） 相关度：13.1 正文：37620 字 / 2 图

命中：mesh

Branching Walk-on-Spheres (WoS) solves semilinear PDEs without meshes, but its computational cost grows sharply near critical branching rates. We introduce Walk in Envelopes (WiE), which uses certified solution bounds to transform branching diffusion rather than prune existing trees. Walk in Envelopes: Efficient Branching Walk-on-Spheres via Certified Solution Bounds

Yunfeng Liao , , , Affiliation: Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen)ShenzhenGuangdongChina, Zhenhao Qiu , , , Affiliation: Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen)ShenzhenGuangdongChina, Xinyang Chen , , , Affiliation: Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen)ShenzhenGuangdongChina and Xiucheng Li , , , Affiliation: Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen)ShenzhenGuangdongChina© none

Abstract.

Branching Walk-on-Spheres (WoS) solves semilinear PDEs without meshes, but its computational cost grows sharply near critical branching rates. We introduce (WiE), which uses certified solution bounds to transform branching diffusion rather than prune existing trees. The transformation suppresses reproduction, introduces controlled termination, and preserves unbiasedness with an envelope-dependent variance bound. We realize the transformed process through exact rejection sampling using standard screened WoS kernels, supported by certified spline envelopes and adaptive sampling and further prove that suitable harmonic envelopes yield bounded expected reproduction counts even as conventional BBM diverges.Walk in Envelopes

Walk-on-Spheres, Branching Brownian Motion, Semilinear PDEs, Certified Solution Bounds, Monte Carlo Methods

Keywords:

1.

Grid-free Monte Carlo methods have become an attractive alternative to mesh-based PDE solvers, enabling pointwise solution queries on complex domains without constructing a global discretization . While Walk-on-Spheres (WoS) efficiently resolves linear elliptic equations through boundary-hitting processes, extending this paradigm to semilinear PDEs requires handling nonlinear reactions. Branching Brownian motion (BBM) provides a natural probabilistic representation by replacing nonlinear terms with particle reproduction events . Combined with WoS, this yields a grid-free solver for semilinear equations. However, eliminating Brownian time discretization does not eliminate branching complexity: each offspring initiates additional walks, and the expected particle population diverges as the branching intensity approaches a critical spectral threshold. This makes otherwise valid stochastic representations increasingly expensive precisely in strongly nonlinear regimes.()Sawhney and Crane, 2020()Agarwal and Claisse, 2020

A natural strategy is to exploit approximate solution information to terminate branches whose remaining contributions are sufficiently small. Yet such pruning requires reliable bounds on unresolved subtrees, whose evaluation can itself be expensive. Approximate bounds may also introduce bias, while tighter estimates do not necessarily offset their computation costs. More fundamentally, pruning acts on a branching process that has already been generated, rather than preventing unnecessary reproduction. This motivates a different question: can certified solution information be used to construct an equivalent stochastic process that branches less frequently, without sacrificing correctness?

We introduce (WiE), a branching WoS framework that transforms the stochastic representation using certified lower and upper solution envelopes. Given sub- and supersolutions , we normalize the unknown solution as . This induces a generalized Doob transform whose diffusion, reproduction, and termination mechanisms are determined by the envelope functions. For binary branching, the reproduction rate becomes , while envelope residuals introduce additional success and failure termination events. The resulting estimator remains unbiased and has variance bounded by . Moreover, we characterize its expected reproduction count through an elliptic equation, showing that a suitable harmonic envelope can keep this count uniformly bounded even as conventional BBM approaches its critical divergence threshold. Although branching-process transformations have established mathematical foundations , WiE develops them into a certified computational framework for semilinear PDE solving.Walk in Envelopesℓ≤u≤a\ell\leq u\leq av=(u−ℓ)/(a−ℓ)v=(u-\ell)/(a-\ell)λ⁡(a−ℓ)\lambda(a-\ell)(a−ℓ)2/4(a-\ell)^{2}/4()Engländer, 2007

The transformed process introduces spatially varying diffusion, which would ordinarily require simulating drifted trajectories. We avoid this difficulty by deriving an exact envelope-aware transition using the original screened WoS exit and Green kernels. Rejection sampling with certified local majorants realizes the transformed distribution without evaluating weighted kernel integrals. To obtain useful envelopes efficiently, we develop monotone refinement of cubic B-spline sub- and supersolutions, using Bernstein constraints to certify PDE inequalities throughout the domain by comparison principle. Adaptive screening, spatially localized rejection bounds, and lazy evaluation further reduce sampling overhead, while a spectral-workload criterion avoids unnecessary preprocessing in inexpensive regimes.

We evaluate WiE on four complex two-dimensional domains across branching intensities and accuracy requirements. Near criticality, WiE achieves – improvements in time–variance efficiency and – reductions in sampling time at matched accuracy, excluding one-time envelope construction. Its benefits increase with branching intensity, while a workload-aware fallback preserves the efficiency of conventional BBM in easier regimes. We additionally demonstrate extensions to projected walks on manifolds and semilinear parabolic equations.6.96.916.2×16.2\times4.74.714.6×14.6\times

Our main contributions are:

  • •

    A certified envelope transformation of branching diffusion, with unbiased estimation, variance guarantees, and a spectral characterization of near-critical branching complexity.

  • •

    An exact envelope-aware WoS sampler using existing screened kernels, without explicitly simulating transformed diffusion.

  • •

    A practical solver combining certified spline-envelope refinement, efficient rejection sampling, and workload-aware fallback, with substantial near-critical acceleration.

    Branching Diffusions and Solution-Guided Transformations.

    BBM represents semilinear reaction–diffusion PDEs, beginning with McKean’s Kolmogorov–Petrovskii–Piskunov representation . Branching-diffusion solvers extend to polynomial nonlinearities, gradient dependence via marked particles , and elliptic boundary-value problems on bounded domains , but face integrability and branching-cost restrictions under strong branching. Process transformations are well established: nonlinear -transforms alter both motion and reproduction , while measure changes and backbone decompositions characterize conditioned branching and near-critical behavior . These underpin solution-guided representations. Our computational realization uses certified sub- and supersolutions to obtain nonnegative branching and killing rates, with exact sphere-transition sampling requiring neither the unknown solution nor drifted-trajectory simulation.()McKean, 1975()Henry-Labordère et al., 2019()Agarwal and Claisse, 2020hh()Engländer, 2007(; )Salisbury and Verzani, 2000Harris et al., 2016

    Monte Carlo Methods for Nonlinear Equations.

    Monte Carlo solvers avoid global spatial discretization, but nested nonlinear expectations and recursive branching can sharply increase variance and work. Numerical branching methods handle polynomial nonlinear PDEs, subject to representation-dependent convergence and integrability . In graphics, accelerate nonlinear recursive light transport through nonlinear path filtering that reuses intermediate evaluations and neural radiance caching that learns them. For nonlinear radiative boundary conditions, combine Picard-style iteration with Monte Carlo PDE solvers. These reduce nonlinear integral-equation costs through reuse, approximation, or iteration. Instead, we retain a branching estimator but change its probability law: certified envelopes suppress reproduction, bound its range, and preserve its expectation under stated assumptions. We reduce sample-generation work rather than only accelerate or approximate an existing recursion.(; )Henry-Labordère et al., 2019Agarwal and Claisse, 2020()Tong and Hachisuka, 2025()Bao et al., 2026

    Walk-on-Spheres and Grid-Free PDE Solvers.

    WoS originated for Dirichlet problems and entered geometric computing as a grid-free elliptic PDE solver for point queries . Extensions handle spatially varying coefficients via null scattering , mixed Neumann–Dirichlet conditions via walk on stars , and boundary-integral transport via walk on boundary . Boundary-value caching reuses estimates across queries , differential WoS computes parameter derivatives , and projected walks solve surface PDEs . These advances mainly address linear PDE representations, boundary handling, or stochastic-estimate reuse. For semilinear PDEs, sphere jumps eliminate Brownian time discretization but not branching-tree growth. We target this remaining bottleneck through certified semilinear bounds and a transformed process with weighted exit and interior events sampled using the original screened WoS kernels.()Muller, 1956()Sawhney and Crane, 2020()Sawhney et al., 2022()Sawhney et al., 2023()Sugimoto et al., 2023()Miller et al., 2023()Miller et al., 2024()Sugimoto et al., 2024a
