Walk in Envelopes: Efficient Branching Walk-on-Spheres via Certified Solution Bounds

Yunfeng Liao , , , Affiliation: Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen)ShenzhenGuangdongChina, Zhenhao Qiu , , , Affiliation: Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen)ShenzhenGuangdongChina, Xinyang Chen , , , Affiliation: Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen)ShenzhenGuangdongChina and Xiucheng Li , , , Affiliation: Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen)ShenzhenGuangdongChina© none

Abstract.

Branching Walk-on-Spheres (WoS) solves semilinear PDEs without meshes, but its computational cost grows sharply near critical branching rates. We introduce (WiE), which uses certified solution bounds to transform branching diffusion rather than prune existing trees. The transformation suppresses reproduction, introduces controlled termination, and preserves unbiasedness with an envelope-dependent variance bound. We realize the transformed process through exact rejection sampling using standard screened WoS kernels, supported by certified spline envelopes and adaptive sampling and further prove that suitable harmonic envelopes yield bounded expected reproduction counts even as conventional BBM diverges.Walk in Envelopes

Walk-on-Spheres, Branching Brownian Motion, Semilinear PDEs, Certified Solution Bounds, Monte Carlo Methods

Keywords:

1.

Grid-free Monte Carlo methods have become an attractive alternative to mesh-based PDE solvers, enabling pointwise solution queries on complex domains without constructing a global discretization . While Walk-on-Spheres (WoS) efficiently resolves linear elliptic equations through boundary-hitting processes, extending this paradigm to semilinear PDEs requires handling nonlinear reactions. Branching Brownian motion (BBM) provides a natural probabilistic representation by replacing nonlinear terms with particle reproduction events . Combined with WoS, this yields a grid-free solver for semilinear equations. However, eliminating Brownian time discretization does not eliminate branching complexity: each offspring initiates additional walks, and the expected particle population diverges as the branching intensity approaches a critical spectral threshold. This makes otherwise valid stochastic representations increasingly expensive precisely in strongly nonlinear regimes.()Sawhney and Crane, 2020()Agarwal and Claisse, 2020

A natural strategy is to exploit approximate solution information to terminate branches whose remaining contributions are sufficiently small. Yet such pruning requires reliable bounds on unresolved subtrees, whose evaluation can itself be expensive. Approximate bounds may also introduce bias, while tighter estimates do not necessarily offset their computation costs. More fundamentally, pruning acts on a branching process that has already been generated, rather than preventing unnecessary reproduction. This motivates a different question: can certified solution information be used to construct an equivalent stochastic process that branches less frequently, without sacrificing correctness?

We introduce (WiE), a branching WoS framework that transforms the stochastic representation using certified lower and upper solution envelopes. Given sub- and supersolutions , we normalize the unknown solution as . This induces a generalized Doob transform whose diffusion, reproduction, and termination mechanisms are determined by the envelope functions. For binary branching, the reproduction rate becomes , while envelope residuals introduce additional success and failure termination events. The resulting estimator remains unbiased and has variance bounded by . Moreover, we characterize its expected reproduction count through an elliptic equation, showing that a suitable harmonic envelope can keep this count uniformly bounded even as conventional BBM approaches its critical divergence threshold. Although branching-process transformations have established mathematical foundations , WiE develops them into a certified computational framework for semilinear PDE solving.Walk in Envelopesℓ≤u≤a\ell\leq u\leq av=(u−ℓ)/(a−ℓ)v=(u-\ell)/(a-\ell)λ⁡(a−ℓ)\lambda(a-\ell)(a−ℓ)2/4(a-\ell)^{2}/4()Engländer, 2007

The transformed process introduces spatially varying diffusion, which would ordinarily require simulating drifted trajectories. We avoid this difficulty by deriving an exact envelope-aware transition using the original screened WoS exit and Green kernels. Rejection sampling with certified local majorants realizes the transformed distribution without evaluating weighted kernel integrals. To obtain useful envelopes efficiently, we develop monotone refinement of cubic B-spline sub- and supersolutions, using Bernstein constraints to certify PDE inequalities throughout the domain by comparison principle. Adaptive screening, spatially localized rejection bounds, and lazy evaluation further reduce sampling overhead, while a spectral-workload criterion avoids unnecessary preprocessing in inexpensive regimes.

We evaluate WiE on four complex two-dimensional domains across branching intensities and accuracy requirements. Near criticality, WiE achieves – improvements in time–variance efficiency and – reductions in sampling time at matched accuracy, excluding one-time envelope construction. Its benefits increase with branching intensity, while a workload-aware fallback preserves the efficiency of conventional BBM in easier regimes. We additionally demonstrate extensions to projected walks on manifolds and semilinear parabolic equations.6.96.916.2×16.2\times4.74.714.6×14.6\times

Our main contributions are:

  • •

    A certified envelope transformation of branching diffusion, with unbiased estimation, variance guarantees, and a spectral characterization of near-critical branching complexity.

  • •

    An exact envelope-aware WoS sampler using existing screened kernels, without explicitly simulating transformed diffusion.

  • •

    A practical solver combining certified spline-envelope refinement, efficient rejection sampling, and workload-aware fallback, with substantial near-critical acceleration.

    • 2.

    Branching Diffusions and Solution-Guided Transformations.

    BBM represents semilinear reaction–diffusion PDEs, beginning with McKean’s Kolmogorov–Petrovskii–Piskunov representation . Branching-diffusion solvers extend to polynomial nonlinearities, gradient dependence via marked particles , and elliptic boundary-value problems on bounded domains , but face integrability and branching-cost restrictions under strong branching. Process transformations are well established: nonlinear -transforms alter both motion and reproduction , while measure changes and backbone decompositions characterize conditioned branching and near-critical behavior . These underpin solution-guided representations. Our computational realization uses certified sub- and supersolutions to obtain nonnegative branching and killing rates, with exact sphere-transition sampling requiring neither the unknown solution nor drifted-trajectory simulation.()McKean, 1975()Henry-Labordère et al., 2019()Agarwal and Claisse, 2020hh()Engländer, 2007(; )Salisbury and Verzani, 2000Harris et al., 2016

    Monte Carlo Methods for Nonlinear Equations.

    Monte Carlo solvers avoid global spatial discretization, but nested nonlinear expectations and recursive branching can sharply increase variance and work. Numerical branching methods handle polynomial nonlinear PDEs, subject to representation-dependent convergence and integrability . In graphics, accelerate nonlinear recursive light transport through nonlinear path filtering that reuses intermediate evaluations and neural radiance caching that learns them. For nonlinear radiative boundary conditions, combine Picard-style iteration with Monte Carlo PDE solvers. These reduce nonlinear integral-equation costs through reuse, approximation, or iteration. Instead, we retain a branching estimator but change its probability law: certified envelopes suppress reproduction, bound its range, and preserve its expectation under stated assumptions. We reduce sample-generation work rather than only accelerate or approximate an existing recursion.(; )Henry-Labordère et al., 2019Agarwal and Claisse, 2020()Tong and Hachisuka, 2025()Bao et al., 2026

    Walk-on-Spheres and Grid-Free PDE Solvers.

    WoS originated for Dirichlet problems and entered geometric computing as a grid-free elliptic PDE solver for point queries . Extensions handle spatially varying coefficients via null scattering , mixed Neumann–Dirichlet conditions via walk on stars , and boundary-integral transport via walk on boundary . Boundary-value caching reuses estimates across queries , differential WoS computes parameter derivatives , and projected walks solve surface PDEs . These advances mainly address linear PDE representations, boundary handling, or stochastic-estimate reuse. For semilinear PDEs, sphere jumps eliminate Brownian time discretization but not branching-tree growth. We target this remaining bottleneck through certified semilinear bounds and a transformed process with weighted exit and interior events sampled using the original screened WoS kernels.()Muller, 1956()Sawhney and Crane, 2020()Sawhney et al., 2022()Sawhney et al., 2023()Sugimoto et al., 2023()Miller et al., 2023()Miller et al., 2024()Sugimoto et al., 2024a

License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.19520v1 [cs.CV] 14 Oct 2026

Spectral World Renderer: Unified 3D Hyperspectral Unmixing

Chia-Ming Lee University at Albany, State University of New York Affiliation: Yu-Jou Hsiao National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University National Cheng Kung UniversityAffiliation: https://ming053l.github.io/Spectral-World-Renderer/Ming-Ching Chang University at Albany, State University of New York Affiliation: Xin Li University at Albany, State University of New York Affiliation: Yu-Lun Liu Chih-Chung Hsu National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University National Cheng Kung UniversityAffiliation: https://ming053l.github.io/Spectral-World-Renderer/

Abstract

Cameras and the foundation models built on them recognize what a 3D scene contains, but not what it is made of: surfaces of the same colour can be different materials. Hyperspectral unmixing explains each spectrum as a mixture of material signatures, yet in 3D it is applied to rendered images after the views are composited, or tied to slow implicit fields, and no multi-view data with known composition exist to check the result. We present the Spectral World Renderer (SWR), which unifies world generation and unmixing. A coding agent builds executable 3D worlds that are rendered with measured spectra, so every hyperspectral image comes with exact labels and sub-pixel proportions; the resulting SWR-Bench provides eight indoor and outdoor worlds in which decompositions can be verified. SWR then unmixes inside rendering: each Gaussian of a compact 3D representation is decoded into material abundances before compositing, so one render yields spectra and material maps, and any surface can be queried by material name, a clicked pixel or a reference spectrum. Without material labels, SWR identifies materials best in all eight worlds, has the best mean PSNR on real captures, trains – faster than unmixing baselines, renders 34.9 labelled views/s and separates same-coloured materials.3.73.712.9×12.9\times

1

Knowing what a scene is made of, not only what it contains, matters for robotic sorting, agriculture and building inspection. Foundation models such as CLIP, SAM and DINOv2 recognize and segment objects from RGB images, and their features lift into 3D for open-vocabulary queries . They remain weak at identifying materials: three colours cannot separate surfaces of similar colour but different composition, such as green paint and a leaf; their labels name objects rather than materials, and one object may combine wood, laminate and metal; and they assign one category per pixel, like RGB material segmenters , whereas materials mix within a pixel.[, , , ]67416038[, , ]48449

Hyperspectral imaging supplies the missing evidence: the shape of a reflectance spectrum over tens to hundreds of bands characterizes the material , and spectral unmixing explains each spectrum as a non-negative mixture of material signatures, or endmembers . Extended to 3D, unmixing would reveal which materials each surface point contains, consistently across views.[, , , ]22204253[]5

This extension is difficult. , so representations that store a spectrum per primitive grow with the band count. : within a pixel, as in 2D, and along each ray; unmixing rendered spectra afterwards cannot separate what compositing has mixed. : illumination changes the brightness and shape of a spectrum, and a model can explain two similar materials with one endmember while intensity absorbs their difference.(1) Hyperspectral data have many bands(2) Mixing occurs twice(3) The decomposition is ambiguous

Existing methods treat reconstruction and unmixing as separate steps. reconstruct spectra, often storing per-band quantities on every primitive, and are evaluated mainly by spectral fidelity; materials are then estimated by unmixing their renderings. unmixes inside a radiance field, but its implicit field makes training and rendering slow and lacks queryable primitives. Moreover, as Table  shows, the data needed to verify a decomposition are missing: are tabletop or turntable captures  that record radiance but no material labels or sub-pixel proportions, which cannot be annotated reliably by hand, and contain geometry and semantics, not spectra.Spectral radiance fields and Gaussian splatting[, , , , , , ]9478258247655UnMix-NeRF[]631real multi-view hyperspectral datasets[, , ]40944synthetic RGB datasets

We therefore generate worlds whose composition is known by construction. In the world generator of our Spectral World Renderer (SWR), shown in Figure , a coding agent turns reference images and text into executable scene programs that fix geometry, materials, illumination and cameras. Measured spectra ground the materials, and shared sub-pixel samples render aligned RGB and hyperspectral observations, material labels and proportions. SWR-Bench offers eight worlds that separate fidelity from identity.2

Spectral World Renderer unifies unmixing with rendering in Gaussian splatting and targets each difficulty. instead of a spectrum, so storage does not grow with the bands. to abundances over a scene-wide endmember dictionary, so mixing is resolved before compositing and one render yields both. keeps it from merging materials by assigning over-complete endmembers to distinct appearances without material labels. With abundances on every Gaussian, a material is queried by name, click, reference spectrum or band in 3 ms. SWR has the best mIoU in every world and trains – faster than unmixing baselines on City. Known composition also exposes what fidelity hides: in Market and Study, 3DGS with post-hoc unmixing reaches a lower spectral angle yet far lower mIoU. Our contributions are:(1) An RGB-trained anchor provides compact geometry, and each Gaussian stores a band-independent feature(2) A shared decoder maps this feature, at every ray intersection,(3) A separate intensity absorbs shading, and a multi-view appearance regularization3.73.712.9×12.9\times

  • •

  • •

  • •

    by name, click, reference spectrum or band, consistent across views, that separate RGB metamers and resist shadow.Real-time material queries

    • 2

    Radiance fields use neural or grid models ; 3DGS composites Gaussians , later improved in quality and speed . Foundation-model features answer object queries and select materials in RGB , and neural harmonic textures vary appearance within a primitive . Hyperspectral fields render radiance per wavelength ; Gaussian versions store spectral quantities per primitive . RGB inverse rendering recovers reflectance and illumination or reflection components . These methods model appearance, spectra or objects; SWR also reveals materials.Hyperspectral 3D reconstruction.[, , ]56257[]37[, , , , ]9132527125[, ]6741[, , , , ]389566889[]17[]12[, , , ]4794044[, , , , ]8258245576[, , ]69350[]85

    Unmixing explains each spectrum by endmembers and non-negative abundances , found by geometric extraction , factorization or autoencoders , with spatial regularization or spectral-variability and nonlinear models . These 2D abundance maps serve remote sensing and material analysis . UnMix-NeRF brings unmixing into a radiance field . Like it, SWR learns endmembers and abundances jointly, but on explicit Gaussians and before compositing.Spectral unmixing.[, , ]39526[, ]8759[, , ]466279[]35[, ]2927[, ]6520[]63

    Procedural rules , language-model layouts and scene code build 3D worlds. Programmable and generative world renderers turn scene state or G-buffers into video . None models spectra or proportions; the SWR world generator binds measured spectra to inspectable geometry, sampling images with their composition.Programmatic world generation.[, ]6869[, ]1688[, ]3148[, , ]333451

    Synthetic and scanned datasets supply geometry, semantics or intrinsic images ; game and agent benchmarks add G-buffers and checkable scene code . Spectral renderers and remote-sensing simulators trace light per wavelength , and ray-traced vegetation scenes give known abundances for 2D unmixing . As Table  summarizes, none pairs multi-view spectra with area proportions; SWR-Bench samples both from the same sub-pixel points, varies specimens and illumination, and stores coefficients so every target can be regenerated.Synthetic benchmarks and spectral simulation.[, , ]787323[, , , ]34199074[, , , ]64863621[]131

The renderer (Sec. ) unmixes at every ray intersection, so one render yields spectra, abundances and material queries at any band count; it uses , and (Sec. ). Training uses no material labels; validation labels only select the number of endmembers .3.1indoor and outdoor worldslabels and sub-pixel proportionsmeasured spectra3.2band-independent featuresdecoding before compositinga separate intensity with multi-view appearance regularization3.3KK

    Scoring an unmixing needs the material proportions of every pixel, which real captures cannot provide. The SWR world generator therefore renders images, material labels and area proportions from the same camera samples, so every target follows from the scene (Figure ).2

Some worlds go beyond this Lambertian model: NVIDIA HQ adds rough specular highlights, a glass reflection and a hazy analytic sky; Karst water adds reflection, refraction and absorption; the interiors are path traced in Mitsuba . Each effect is stored separately.AcA_{c}cckk[]36

    Reflectance comes from ECOSTRESS and USGS measurements , and every assignment is recorded, so each observation can be traced to the spectra that produced it. No single spectrum describes a whole material: specimens differ within a class, and sunlight and skylight change the spectral shape of one surface, as Figure (a,b) shows. Each surface keeps one specimen across views. Outdoor worlds use ASTM G173 sunlight and skylight , interiors white sources . We render 64 bands from 420 to 980 nm, clean and with shot and read noise .Measured spectra and their variation.[, ]53423[]1[]11[]18

    Ground truth must be exact, so each world is checked for label alignment and integrity, spectral provenance and train/test separation. Stored coefficients and contributions re-compose clean outdoor radiance, indoor transport is checked before adding noise, and assigned spectra lie within independent library measurements (Figure (c)).Verification.3

    3.2

    Unmixing a rendered image afterwards acts on spectra that compositing has already mixed. Spectral World Renderer instead unmixes inside rendering: at every ray intersection, a shared decoder turns the local feature into abundances and an intensity, and compositing accumulates both, so one render yields spectra and abundances (Figure ).4

    Hyperspectral observations are noisy and vary with illumination, and across many views these errors also degrade the recovered geometry. We therefore fit the geometry as a 3DGS anchor on co-registered RGB images, supplied with the data or derived from visible-band responses; advances in RGB Gaussian splatting thus transfer directly. FastGS densification and pruning  keep only primitives supported across views, so rendering is faster and fewer features and intersections remain to optimize and unmix. Unlike HyperGS , the anchor requires no spectral autoencoder. It has Gaussians with mean , rotation , scale and opacity ; after fitting, we drop colours and fold the rasterizer’s screen-space variance into the scales. Instead of a spectrum, each Gaussian carries a neural harmonic texture , whose variation inside the primitive lets few Gaussians represent fine detail: four feature vectors , , with .     Accurate spectra do not imply a correct decomposition. Eq.  fits each spectrum but does not fix which endmember explains it. Two similar materials may share one endmember while the intensity absorbs their brightness difference, like the scaling factors of extended mixing models ; the spectra are reconstructed well, yet the materials merge in .     SWR-Bench has eight indoor and outdoor worlds of known composition. For materials, we compare UnMix-NeRF and an -channel 3DGS unmixed afterwards with VCA endmembers from training-view renders and NNLS . For fidelity, we add HyperGS and DD-HGS .     4.1

    A lower SAM does not imply better labels. On Market and Study, 3DGS reaches a lower SAM than SWR yet a far lower mIoU, as Table  and Figure  show: unmixing afterwards works on contributions that compositing has already mixed.     4.2

    Refinement on the fixed anchor is cheap: it takes 36.5 s of the 397 s City pipeline, yet refining geometry and feature layout improves Market by 2.9 dB and 0.12 mIoU and the real apple by 2.6 dB, as Table  shows.RGB feature stage.3

    A Gaussian crossing an edge or shadow needs more than one mixture, as Figure  tests on Market without . One feature per Gaussian costs 1.6 dB and lowers mIoU from 0.47 to 0.34. Fixed intensity keeps PSNR but lowers mIoU to 0.22, as mixtures absorb shading.Within-primitive variation.7ℒp\mathcal{L}_{p}

    Decoding after compositing raises Market PSNR from 33.72 to 34.37 dB yet lowers mIoU from 0.47 to 0.37 (Table S7): ray-averaged features blend surfaces, as unmixing afterwards does in Table .Unmixing inside rendering.2

    Rare materials remain hard. Appearance regularization recovers Forbidden City marble (Figure (c)) but misses ink in Study, which NNLS with the true class spectra mostly separates (Figure S7).Material allocation limits.5

    4.3

    SWR has the highest PSNR on each real dataset in Table . Its margin is largest on the 204-band apple in Figure , where PSNR, mean SAM and p95 all improve over HyperGS; on HS-NeRF, 3DGS has a lower mean and p95 angle.Fidelity without material truth.58

    SWR is fastest in Table : City trains in 6 min 37 s versus 24 min for UnMix-NeRF and 85 min for 3DGS+VCA/NNLS, and our optimized fused fp16 decoder renders 34.9 views/s with label maps.Efficiency.4

    4.4

    Leaves have a red edge near 700 nm: chlorophyll absorbs red light and leaf tissue reflects near-infrared. Minerals and dry leaves lack it, so foliage-coloured mineral leaves ( apart in RGB, in spectrum) and dry crowns get their own endmembers, as Figure (b,c) shows.Seeing beyond RGB.2∘2^{\circ}42∘42^{\circ}9

    In hyperspectral images, such materials are usually isolated by supervised classifiers  or by unsupervised subspace clustering , which need labels or a run per image. SWR needs neither: abundances live on explicit, rasterizable Gaussians, so a material query selects primitives, consistently across views. The mineral-leaf query retrieves no ordinary tree, whereas the RGB query retrieves eleven, as Figure (a) shows. A measured spectrum can also serve as the query. With sun and sky illumination factored out, a pixel clicked in shadow retrieves 77 % of the sunlit part of its material, against 10 % for RGB (mean over four outdoor worlds, 3 ms per query; Sec. I), as Figure (d) shows.Querying primitives directly.[, , , ]54811028[]9299

    5

    Spectral World Renderer brings hyperspectral unmixing into 3D as one verifiable framework: its world generator renders images with their exact material composition, and its renderer unmixes at every ray intersection, so a single render yields spectra and material maps checkable against known truth. Without material labels, SWR identifies materials best in all eight worlds and has the best mean PSNR on real captures; it trains City in under seven minutes, renders 34.9 labelled views/s, and its per-Gaussian abundances answer queries by name, click, reference spectrum or band, even for same-coloured materials. Future work will enrich light transport and sensor models, allocate endmembers to rare materials and handle dynamic scenes.

Spectral World Renderer: Unified 3D Hyperspectral Unmixing

Chia-Ming Lee University at Albany, State University of New York Affiliation: Yu-Jou Hsiao National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University National Cheng Kung UniversityAffiliation: https://ming053l.github.io/Spectral-World-Renderer/Ming-Ching Chang University at Albany, State University of New York Affiliation: Xin Li University at Albany, State University of New York Affiliation: Yu-Lun Liu Chih-Chung Hsu National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University National Cheng Kung UniversityAffiliation: https://ming053l.github.io/Spectral-World-Renderer/

Abstract

Cameras and the foundation models built on them recognize what a 3D scene contains, but not what it is made of: surfaces of the same colour can be different materials. Hyperspectral unmixing explains each spectrum as a mixture of material signatures, yet in 3D it is applied to rendered images after the views are composited, or tied to slow implicit fields, and no multi-view data with known composition exist to check the result. We present the Spectral World Renderer (SWR), which unifies world generation and unmixing. A coding agent builds executable 3D worlds that are rendered with measured spectra, so every hyperspectral image comes with exact labels and sub-pixel proportions; the resulting SWR-Bench provides eight indoor and outdoor worlds in which decompositions can be verified. SWR then unmixes inside rendering: each Gaussian of a compact 3D representation is decoded into material abundances before compositing, so one render yields spectra and material maps, and any surface can be queried by material name, a clicked pixel or a reference spectrum. Without material labels, SWR identifies materials best in all eight worlds, has the best mean PSNR on real captures, trains – faster than unmixing baselines, renders 34.9 labelled views/s and separates same-coloured materials.3.73.712.9×12.9\times

1

Knowing what a scene is made of, not only what it contains, matters for robotic sorting, agriculture and building inspection. Foundation models such as CLIP, SAM and DINOv2 recognize and segment objects from RGB images, and their features lift into 3D for open-vocabulary queries . They remain weak at identifying materials: three colours cannot separate surfaces of similar colour but different composition, such as green paint and a leaf; their labels name objects rather than materials, and one object may combine wood, laminate and metal; and they assign one category per pixel, like RGB material segmenters , whereas materials mix within a pixel.[, , , ]67416038[, , ]48449

Hyperspectral imaging supplies the missing evidence: the shape of a reflectance spectrum over tens to hundreds of bands characterizes the material , and spectral unmixing explains each spectrum as a non-negative mixture of material signatures, or endmembers . Extended to 3D, unmixing would reveal which materials each surface point contains, consistently across views.[, , , ]22204253[]5

This extension is difficult. , so representations that store a spectrum per primitive grow with the band count. : within a pixel, as in 2D, and along each ray; unmixing rendered spectra afterwards cannot separate what compositing has mixed. : illumination changes the brightness and shape of a spectrum, and a model can explain two similar materials with one endmember while intensity absorbs their difference.(1) Hyperspectral data have many bands(2) Mixing occurs twice(3) The decomposition is ambiguous

Existing methods treat reconstruction and unmixing as separate steps. reconstruct spectra, often storing per-band quantities on every primitive, and are evaluated mainly by spectral fidelity; materials are then estimated by unmixing their renderings. unmixes inside a radiance field, but its implicit field makes training and rendering slow and lacks queryable primitives. Moreover, as Table  shows, the data needed to verify a decomposition are missing: are tabletop or turntable captures  that record radiance but no material labels or sub-pixel proportions, which cannot be annotated reliably by hand, and contain geometry and semantics, not spectra.Spectral radiance fields and Gaussian splatting[, , , , , , ]9478258247655UnMix-NeRF[]631real multi-view hyperspectral datasets[, , ]40944synthetic RGB datasets

We therefore generate worlds whose composition is known by construction. In the world generator of our Spectral World Renderer (SWR), shown in Figure , a coding agent turns reference images and text into executable scene programs that fix geometry, materials, illumination and cameras. Measured spectra ground the materials, and shared sub-pixel samples render aligned RGB and hyperspectral observations, material labels and proportions. SWR-Bench offers eight worlds that separate fidelity from identity.2

Spectral World Renderer unifies unmixing with rendering in Gaussian splatting and targets each difficulty. instead of a spectrum, so storage does not grow with the bands. to abundances over a scene-wide endmember dictionary, so mixing is resolved before compositing and one render yields both. keeps it from merging materials by assigning over-complete endmembers to distinct appearances without material labels. With abundances on every Gaussian, a material is queried by name, click, reference spectrum or band in 3 ms. SWR has the best mIoU in every world and trains – faster than unmixing baselines on City. Known composition also exposes what fidelity hides: in Market and Study, 3DGS with post-hoc unmixing reaches a lower spectral angle yet far lower mIoU. Our contributions are:(1) An RGB-trained anchor provides compact geometry, and each Gaussian stores a band-independent feature(2) A shared decoder maps this feature, at every ray intersection,(3) A separate intensity absorbs shading, and a multi-view appearance regularization3.73.712.9×12.9\times

    • 2

    Radiance fields use neural or grid models ; 3DGS composites Gaussians , later improved in quality and speed . Foundation-model features answer object queries and select materials in RGB , and neural harmonic textures vary appearance within a primitive . Hyperspectral fields render radiance per wavelength ; Gaussian versions store spectral quantities per primitive . RGB inverse rendering recovers reflectance and illumination or reflection components . These methods model appearance, spectra or objects; SWR also reveals materials.Hyperspectral 3D reconstruction.[, , ]56257[]37[, , , , ]9132527125[, ]6741[, , , , ]389566889[]17[]12[, , , ]4794044[, , , , ]8258245576[, , ]69350[]85

    Unmixing explains each spectrum by endmembers and non-negative abundances , found by geometric extraction , factorization or autoencoders , with spatial regularization or spectral-variability and nonlinear models . These 2D abundance maps serve remote sensing and material analysis . UnMix-NeRF brings unmixing into a radiance field . Like it, SWR learns endmembers and abundances jointly, but on explicit Gaussians and before compositing.Spectral unmixing.[, , ]39526[, ]8759[, , ]466279[]35[, ]2927[, ]6520[]63

    Procedural rules , language-model layouts and scene code build 3D worlds. Programmable and generative world renderers turn scene state or G-buffers into video . None models spectra or proportions; the SWR world generator binds measured spectra to inspectable geometry, sampling images with their composition.Programmatic world generation.[, ]6869[, ]1688[, ]3148[, , ]333451

    Synthetic and scanned datasets supply geometry, semantics or intrinsic images ; game and agent benchmarks add G-buffers and checkable scene code . Spectral renderers and remote-sensing simulators trace light per wavelength , and ray-traced vegetation scenes give known abundances for 2D unmixing . As Table  summarizes, none pairs multi-view spectra with area proportions; SWR-Bench samples both from the same sub-pixel points, varies specimens and illumination, and stores coefficients so every target can be regenerated.Synthetic benchmarks and spectral simulation.[, , ]787323[, , , ]34199074[, , , ]64863621[]131

    Unmixing a rendered image afterwards acts on spectra that compositing has already mixed. We therefore fit the geometry as a 3DGS anchor on co-registered RGB images, supplied with the data or derived from visible-band responses; advances in RGB Gaussian splatting thus transfer directly. Instead of a spectrum, each Gaussian carries a neural harmonic texture , whose variation inside the primitive lets few Gaussians represent fine detail: four feature vectors , , with .     A lower SAM does not imply better labels. On Market and Study, 3DGS reaches a lower SAM than SWR yet a far lower mIoU, as Table  and Figure  show: unmixing afterwards works on contributions that compositing has already mixed.     In hyperspectral images, such materials are usually isolated by supervised classifiers  or by unsupervised subspace clustering , which need labels or a run per image. SWR needs neither: abundances live on explicit, rasterizable Gaussians, so a material query selects primitives, consistently across views. The mineral-leaf query retrieves no ordinary tree, whereas the RGB query retrieves eleven, as Figure (a) shows. A measured spectrum can also serve as the query. With sun and sky illumination factored out, a pixel clicked in shadow retrieves 77 % of the sunlit part of its material, against 10 % for RGB (mean over four outdoor worlds, 3 ms per query; Sec. I), as Figure (d) shows.Querying primitives directly.[, , , ]54811028[]9299

    Spectral World Renderer brings hyperspectral unmixing into 3D as one verifiable framework: its world generator renders images with their exact material composition, and its renderer unmixes at every ray intersection, so a single render yields spectra and material maps checkable against known truth. Without material labels, SWR identifies materials best in all eight worlds and has the best mean PSNR on real captures; it trains City in under seven minutes, renders 34.9 labelled views/s, and its per-Gaussian abundances answer queries by name, click, reference spectrum or band, even for same-coloured materials. Future work will enrich light transport and sensor models, allocate endmembers to rare materials and handle dynamic scenes.

item.title: Colour-Field Based Particle Categorization for Residual Stress Detection and Reduction in Solid SPH Simulations
item.description:

命中：particle

Residual stress remains in an object even in the absence of external forces or thermal pressure, which, in turn, may cause significant plastic deformations. In case the residual stress creates unwanted effects on the material and so is undesirable, an efficient solution is necessary to track and eliminate this stress. Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics has been extensively used in solid mechanics sim

[Submitted on 16 Oct 2026]

Title:

Authors:Gizem KayarView PDF
Residual stress remains in an object even in the absence of external forces or thermal pressure, which, in turn, may cause significant plastic deformations. In case the residual stress creates unwanted effects on the material and so is undesirable, an efficient solution is necessary to track and eliminate this stress. Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics has been extensively used in solid mechanics simulations and the inherent colour-field generation approach is a promising tracker for the residual stress. In this paper, we propose a way to use the colour-field approach for eliminating the residual stress and prevent the undesirable premature failure of solid objects. Abstract:

item.title: OrTeN: Neural Inverse Graphics for Joint Terrain and Line-scan Camera Trajectory Reconstruction
item.description:
来源：arXiv·cs.GR 最新（English） 相关度：12.6 正文：31881 字 / 5 图

命中：terrain、rendering、shadow、texture

Digital terrain maps (DTMs) are used for landing site selection, terrain-relative navigation, and geological analysis in planetary exploration. Existing state-of-practice reconstruction techniques for creating DTMs from satellite imagery use multi-view stereo, requiring complex pipelines for dealing with camera error, changing illumination, and images with limited disparity. This work introduces O

License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.24075v1 [cs.CV] 16 Oct 2026

OrTeN: Neural Inverse Graphics for Joint Terrain and Line-scan Camera Trajectory Reconstruction

Josef Biberstein Massachusetts Institute of Technology Affiliation: Email: jxb@mit.eduSertac Karaman Massachusetts Institute of Technology Affiliation: Email: sertac@mit.edu

Abstract

Digital terrain maps (DTMs) are used for landing site selection, terrain-relative navigation, and geological analysis in planetary exploration. Existing state-of-practice reconstruction techniques for creating DTMs from satellite imagery use multi-view stereo, requiring complex pipelines for dealing with camera error, changing illumination, and images with limited disparity. This work introduces Orbital Terrain Networks (OrTeN), a DTM construction method that uses neural inverse rendering to jointly optimize a textured height map and orbital camera corrections from line-scan satellite images. OrTeN operates directly on calibrated line-scan images with pixel values expressed as radiance factor (I/F) and corrects both broad trajectory pose inconsistencies and high-frequency pointing jitter jointly with surface reconstruction during training. Surface-projected patch normalized cross-correlation (NCC) enforces consistency between observations of the same terrain, refining an initial rough reconstruction. A semi-empirical reflectance model and shadow rendering are used to fit surface appearance from multi-date imagery with differing solar illumination. OrTeN requires only calibrated line-scan images and initial camera poses and does not use any structural priors including ranging/depth measurements or initial rough DTMs. OrTeN is evaluated on four planetary imagery datasets. Aligned terrain RMSEs are 2.35 m at Jezero Crater, 2.82 m at Gale Crater, 16.18 m at Olympus Mons, and 0.43 m at McGetchin Crater.

1

Digital terrain maps (DTMs) are an important supporting data product in space exploration. Accurate DTMs enable landing site selection and terrain-relative navigation (TRN) during entry, descent, and landing for modern autonomous space exploration missions such as Mars 2020 . They also provide the topographic context needed to interpret planetary landforms and their geological history .[, ]1121[]29

Current pipelines for orbital DTM production used in the space science community rely on classical multi-view stereo (MVS) techniques to infer terrain structure—features are detected and matched between radiometrically calibrated images, bundle adjustment (BA) is performed to refine camera poses, and stereo correspondences are triangulated to produce a 3D terrain model . MVS can produce high-quality maps suitable for mission operations, but a number of challenges inherent to both MVS itself and its application to satellite datasets complicate the process. These challenges include the difficulty of getting reliable feature matches in the presence of shadows or low-texture regions, the line-scan geometry of most satellite images not admitting the epipolar constraints assumed by traditional MVS, and transients like dust storms or seasonal changes that alter the appearance of the terrain. Correcting for these effects can require labor-intensive preprocessing and careful manual intervention, making MVS pipelines cumbersome to use.[, ]227

Neural inverse graphics provides a methodology for scene reconstruction that can address many of the challenges faced by classical MVS pipelines. For instance, satellite adaptations of neural radiance fields (NeRFs) model changing illumination and acquisition appearance while recovering scene geometry . However, full 3D volumetric representations admit degenerate solutions—for instance, all scene density concentrated in front of cameras, explaining the observed images without recovering the true geometry—which can be particularly problematic when working with low-disparity orbital imagery where depth cues are weak. While structural priors can help mitigate these degeneracies , these measurements are not always available or reliable.[, , ]152627[, ]3836

OrTeN mitigates the shortcomings of classical MVS and volumetric neural reconstruction by optimizing a textured height map directly. Critically, OrTeN requires no structural priors to achieve accurate terrain reconstruction from images and approximate camera poses. It builds on Neural Terrain Maps (NTM) , adding direct bundle adjustment of line-scan camera extrinsics jointly with training, a semi-empirical photometric model, and geometric shadow modeling. The contributions of this work are:[]8

  • 1.

    A pipeline for creating accurate DTMs through differentiable volume rendering of textured height maps including a first-order approximation of distance to the height map along the ray to improve performance at oblique angles.

  • 2.

    Joint terrain and line-scan camera optimization, including smooth trajectory adjustment and high-frequency jitter removal, and a semi-empirical, spatially varying photometric model including geometric shadow modeling with an image-space prior.

  • 3.

    An evaluation on four Mars and Moon scenes with varied relief and illumination, using the Context Camera (CTX) and Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC) Narrow Angle Camera (NAC).

    • OrTeN achieves aligned height errors below the ground sampling distance (GSD) in three scenes and improves on the tested Ames Stereo Pipeline (ASP) reconstruction in those scenes.

    2

    DTM creation with MVS.

    A number of well-established pipelines exist for creating DTMs from orbital imagery using MVS, including the Ames Stereo Pipeline (ASP), satellite stereo pipeline (s2p), and COLMAP . All of these methods use feature extraction and matching to constrain camera alignment before performing dense stereo matching to triangulate terrain. Orbital imagery is often taken by linescan cameras, and therefore integration into standard MVS pipelines requires particular care because each detector line is acquired at a different pose. This precludes the standard epipolar geometry assumptions used in perspective-camera MVS to make searching for correspondences straightforward. Linescan epipolar loci are generally curved, so the global rectification used for ideal perspective cameras must be replaced by local or sensor-specific constructions . ASP can also refine time-varying camera states to correct high-frequency jitter .[, , , ]7133334[, ]1419[]4

    Illumination changes, common in multi-date satellite data acquisitions, create an additional challenge for traditional MVS approaches. Shadows and surface reflectance can change between acquisitions even when terrain is static and make feature selection and matching more difficult. Therefore, masking shadows and other illumination-dependent artifacts is often necessary to improve the robustness of MVS matching. Shadows can also provide important geometric information which can be exploited in reconstruction, and shape-from-shading methods exploit this to further refine existing DTMs . OrTeN performs trajectory bundle adjustment, including jitter removal, jointly with training, and uses a semi-empirical photometric model with explicit geometric shadow handling to improve terrain reconstruction.[]3

    Neural reconstruction of orbital imagery.

    S-NeRF introduced illumination-aware neural rendering for satellite photogrammetry, and Sat-NeRF added rational polynomial coefficient (RPC) camera support and transient appearance modeling. EO-NeRF built on these previous methods to establish a baseline framework for general-purpose scenes on Earth by incorporating geometrically consistent shadows with learned radiometric and camera corrections and transient appearance embeddings . Season-NeRF separated seasonal appearance from Sun and viewing geometry , while a semi-empirical bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF) was incorporated into BRDF-NeRF . Other methods address the geometry directly through depth supervision, surface constraints, or gravity-aligned and coarse-to-fine regularization . Gaussian splatting for satellite imagery has also emerged as an alternative to methods utilizing volume rendering, offering efficient, high-quality neural scene representations .[, , ]152627[]17[]39[, , ]383136[, ]29

    More recent works have begun to focus on large-scale terrain reconstruction using neural inverse graphics. Both NTM and LNEM introduce direct rendering of linescan imagery for terrain reconstruction . For descent imagery, de Almeida . incorporate a neural height field into reconstruction from wide-angle cameras . OrTeN eschews structural priors and retains the explicitly parameterized terrain representation, as is done in NTM, and adds ray-distance-based opacity and improved regularization with normalized cross-correlation (NCC). Its coarse-to-fine optimization follows the principle established by BARF: low-frequency structure should stabilize camera alignment before fine appearance is exposed .[, ]823et al[]12[]24

    3

    OrTeN represents the scene with a height field in a local east–north–up (ENU) frame and learned surface appearance (). The surface is , and unit-direction camera rays are given by . The origin is constructed as the common look point of all cameras, the horizontal bounds are set by the image footprints on the horizontal plane, enlarged by a factor of 1.5, and the vertical bounds are set by global planetary height limits.hθ:ℝ2→ℝh_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{2}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}Fig.2𝐱=(x,y,hθ​(x,y))\mathbf{x}=(x,y,h_{\theta}(x,y))𝐫⁡(t)=𝐨+t​𝐝\mathbf{r}(t)=\mathbf{o}+t\mathbf{d}

    gives the results of the baseline OrTeN configuration on each scene. OrTeN attains sub-GSD height RMSE in Jezero, Gale, and McGetchin scenes.     Depth-supervised EO-NeRF fails to reconstruct accurate DTMs in any of the scenes despite access to structural supervision. It falls short of OrTeN both visually and in structural accuracy. Noting that the default EO-NeRF configuration trains for much longer (300,000 iterations) and takes 10-20 hours to converge, this comparison demonstrates that OrTeN’s approach achieves meaningful improvement in both efficiency and accuracy.

    ASP recovers sound DTMs for all four scenes, but performs worse than OrTeN on all scenes except Olympus Mons. as opposed to ASP, which typically processes images pairwise or in smaller subsets. OrTeN also benefits from its semi-empirical appearance modeling which allows it to better deal with shadows and varying illumination conditions which may confound feature matching in purely photogrammetric approaches.

    Four ablation studies were conducted to evaluate the impact of the three key features in this work: bundle adjustment with jitter, normalized cross-correlation (NCC) for photometric consistency, and semi-empirical appearance modeling with shadow modeling. The results of the ablation are summarized in .Tab.3

    Removing BA significantly degrades the quality of the reconstructed DTMs across all scenes, highlighting the importance of joint optimization of camera parameters and scene geometry. shows baseline and no-BA renderings of the same acquisition for the McGetchin Crater scene. The no-BA ablation shows clearly degraded visual reconstruction quality with a drop of more than 10 dB in reserved-pixel PSNR. The DTM is similarly impacted with RMSE increasing from 0.43 to 10.36 m and the quality of the reconstruction visibly degrading, especially in the fine detail around the central crater region.Fig.4a

    Disabling NCC has an even more pronounced effect on the quality of the reconstructed DTMs. shows baseline and no-NCC renderings of the same acquisition for the Jezero Crater scene, and again illustrates the degradation of fine detail around the crater region. In some of the scenes, the PSNR improves in the no-NCC ablation compared to the baseline. Rendering loss alone can therefore be misleading when assessing terrain reconstruction, especially in low-disparity orbital scenes.Fig.5

    Removal of geometric shadows produces a less pronounced effect on the quality of the reconstructed DTMs compared to the other ablations, but can be observed in reconstruction quality. shows baseline and no-shadow renderings of the same acquisition for the Olympus Mons scene. The baseline is able to reconstruct the large shadow cast by the cliff face while the ablated scene cannot.Fig.6

    5

    OrTeN jointly reconstructs terrain and refines line-scan cameras from calibrated orbital images without depth supervision or stereo initialization. Across four Mars and Moon scenes, it achieves sub-GSD aligned terrain RMSE in three and improves on the tested ASP reconstruction in those same three scenes. The ablations demonstrate the importance of camera refinement and surface-patch NCC for achieving high geometric accuracy. They also show that an accurate image reconstruction can coexist with an incorrect surface. Comparison with EO-NeRF with depth supervision also demonstrates that structural priors are not sufficient to achieve accurate terrain reconstruction efficiently.

    However, a number of limitations remain. Without structural priors such as ranging measurements or known control points, absolute geolocation is not possible. Furthermore, it is possible that integrating structural priors into OrTeN could improve reconstruction accuracy and efficiency and should be tested. While the height map representation is an effective structural prior for the datasets considered here, when detail becomes sufficient, this representation becomes more limiting. For instance, height maps cannot represent overhangs or complex 3D structures like caves. Future work should work on mitigating these shortcomings to allow ground level imagery to be integrated into the terrain reconstruction process.

License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.24075v1 [cs.CV] 16 Oct 2026

OrTeN: Neural Inverse Graphics for Joint Terrain and Line-scan Camera Trajectory Reconstruction

Josef Biberstein Massachusetts Institute of Technology Affiliation: Email: jxb@mit.eduSertac Karaman Massachusetts Institute of Technology Affiliation: Email: sertac@mit.edu

Abstract

Digital terrain maps (DTMs) are used for landing site selection, terrain-relative navigation, and geological analysis in planetary exploration. Existing state-of-practice reconstruction techniques for creating DTMs from satellite imagery use multi-view stereo, requiring complex pipelines for dealing with camera error, changing illumination, and images with limited disparity. This work introduces Orbital Terrain Networks (OrTeN), a DTM construction method that uses neural inverse rendering to jointly optimize a textured height map and orbital camera corrections from line-scan satellite images. OrTeN operates directly on calibrated line-scan images with pixel values expressed as radiance factor (I/F) and corrects both broad trajectory pose inconsistencies and high-frequency pointing jitter jointly with surface reconstruction during training. Surface-projected patch normalized cross-correlation (NCC) enforces consistency between observations of the same terrain, refining an initial rough reconstruction. A semi-empirical reflectance model and shadow rendering are used to fit surface appearance from multi-date imagery with differing solar illumination. OrTeN requires only calibrated line-scan images and initial camera poses and does not use any structural priors including ranging/depth measurements or initial rough DTMs. OrTeN is evaluated on four planetary imagery datasets. Aligned terrain RMSEs are 2.35 m at Jezero Crater, 2.82 m at Gale Crater, 16.18 m at Olympus Mons, and 0.43 m at McGetchin Crater.

1

Digital terrain maps (DTMs) are an important supporting data product in space exploration. Accurate DTMs enable landing site selection and terrain-relative navigation (TRN) during entry, descent, and landing for modern autonomous space exploration missions such as Mars 2020 . They also provide the topographic context needed to interpret planetary landforms and their geological history .[, ]1121[]29

Current pipelines for orbital DTM production used in the space science community rely on classical multi-view stereo (MVS) techniques to infer terrain structure—features are detected and matched between radiometrically calibrated images, bundle adjustment (BA) is performed to refine camera poses, and stereo correspondences are triangulated to produce a 3D terrain model . MVS can produce high-quality maps suitable for mission operations, but a number of challenges inherent to both MVS itself and its application to satellite datasets complicate the process. These challenges include the difficulty of getting reliable feature matches in the presence of shadows or low-texture regions, the line-scan geometry of most satellite images not admitting the epipolar constraints assumed by traditional MVS, and transients like dust storms or seasonal changes that alter the appearance of the terrain. Correcting for these effects can require labor-intensive preprocessing and careful manual intervention, making MVS pipelines cumbersome to use.[, ]227

Neural inverse graphics provides a methodology for scene reconstruction that can address many of the challenges faced by classical MVS pipelines. For instance, satellite adaptations of neural radiance fields (NeRFs) model changing illumination and acquisition appearance while recovering scene geometry . However, full 3D volumetric representations admit degenerate solutions—for instance, all scene density concentrated in front of cameras, explaining the observed images without recovering the true geometry—which can be particularly problematic when working with low-disparity orbital imagery where depth cues are weak. While structural priors can help mitigate these degeneracies , these measurements are not always available or reliable.[, , ]152627[, ]3836

OrTeN mitigates the shortcomings of classical MVS and volumetric neural reconstruction by optimizing a textured height map directly. Critically, OrTeN requires no structural priors to achieve accurate terrain reconstruction from images and approximate camera poses. It builds on Neural Terrain Maps (NTM) , adding direct bundle adjustment of line-scan camera extrinsics jointly with training, a semi-empirical photometric model, and geometric shadow modeling. The contributions of this work are:[]8

  • 1.

    A pipeline for creating accurate DTMs through differentiable volume rendering of textured height maps including a first-order approximation of distance to the height map along the ray to improve performance at oblique angles.

  • 2.

    Joint terrain and line-scan camera optimization, including smooth trajectory adjustment and high-frequency jitter removal, and a semi-empirical, spatially varying photometric model including geometric shadow modeling with an image-space prior.

  • 3.

    An evaluation on four Mars and Moon scenes with varied relief and illumination, using the Context Camera (CTX) and Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC) Narrow Angle Camera (NAC).

    • OrTeN achieves aligned height errors below the ground sampling distance (GSD) in three scenes and improves on the tested Ames Stereo Pipeline (ASP) reconstruction in those scenes.

    2

    DTM creation with MVS.

    A number of well-established pipelines exist for creating DTMs from orbital imagery using MVS, including the Ames Stereo Pipeline (ASP), satellite stereo pipeline (s2p), and COLMAP . All of these methods use feature extraction and matching to constrain camera alignment before performing dense stereo matching to triangulate terrain. Orbital imagery is often taken by linescan cameras, and therefore integration into standard MVS pipelines requires particular care because each detector line is acquired at a different pose. This precludes the standard epipolar geometry assumptions used in perspective-camera MVS to make searching for correspondences straightforward. Linescan epipolar loci are generally curved, so the global rectification used for ideal perspective cameras must be replaced by local or sensor-specific constructions . ASP can also refine time-varying camera states to correct high-frequency jitter .[, , , ]7133334[, ]1419[]4

    Illumination changes, common in multi-date satellite data acquisitions, create an additional challenge for traditional MVS approaches. Shadows and surface reflectance can change between acquisitions even when terrain is static and make feature selection and matching more difficult. Therefore, masking shadows and other illumination-dependent artifacts is often necessary to improve the robustness of MVS matching. Shadows can also provide important geometric information which can be exploited in reconstruction, and shape-from-shading methods exploit this to further refine existing DTMs . OrTeN performs trajectory bundle adjustment, including jitter removal, jointly with training, and uses a semi-empirical photometric model with explicit geometric shadow handling to improve terrain reconstruction.[]3

    Neural reconstruction of orbital imagery.

    S-NeRF introduced illumination-aware neural rendering for satellite photogrammetry, and Sat-NeRF added rational polynomial coefficient (RPC) camera support and transient appearance modeling. EO-NeRF built on these previous methods to establish a baseline framework for general-purpose scenes on Earth by incorporating geometrically consistent shadows with learned radiometric and camera corrections and transient appearance embeddings . Season-NeRF separated seasonal appearance from Sun and viewing geometry , while a semi-empirical bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF) was incorporated into BRDF-NeRF . Other methods address the geometry directly through depth supervision, surface constraints, or gravity-aligned and coarse-to-fine regularization . Gaussian splatting for satellite imagery has also emerged as an alternative to methods utilizing volume rendering, offering efficient, high-quality neural scene representations .[, , ]152627[]17[]39[, , ]383136[, ]29

    More recent works have begun to focus on large-scale terrain reconstruction using neural inverse graphics. Both NTM and LNEM introduce direct rendering of linescan imagery for terrain reconstruction . For descent imagery, de Almeida . incorporate a neural height field into reconstruction from wide-angle cameras . OrTeN eschews structural priors and retains the explicitly parameterized terrain representation, as is done in NTM, and adds ray-distance-based opacity and improved regularization with normalized cross-correlation (NCC). Its coarse-to-fine optimization follows the principle established by BARF: low-frequency structure should stabilize camera alignment before fine appearance is exposed .[, ]823et al[]12[]24

    3

    OrTeN represents the scene with a height field in a local east–north–up (ENU) frame and learned surface appearance (). The surface is , and unit-direction camera rays are given by . The origin is constructed as the common look point of all cameras, the horizontal bounds are set by the image footprints on the horizontal plane, enlarged by a factor of 1.5, and the vertical bounds are set by global planetary height limits.hθ:ℝ2→ℝh_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{2}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}Fig.2𝐱=(x,y,hθ​(x,y))\mathbf{x}=(x,y,h_{\theta}(x,y))𝐫⁡(t)=𝐨+t​𝐝\mathbf{r}(t)=\mathbf{o}+t\mathbf{d}

    This interpolates between Lambert and Lommel–Seeliger responses .[]28

    Geometric shadows.

    Starting from the weighted camera-ray depth, a surface intersection is refined and traced toward the Sun until the ray leaves the scene bounds. Solar interval opacities are converted to visibility usingαk⊙\alpha_{k}^{\odot}

    V=Vatt​∏k(1−αk⊙),Vη=(1−η)​Vatt+η​V.V=V_{\rm att}\prod_{k}(1-\alpha_{k}^{\odot}),\qquad V_{\eta}=(1-\eta)V_{\rm att}+\eta V.(9)

    Here smoothly suppresses light on back-facing slopes and is zero when the Sun is below the local horizon. The startup factor ramps cast shadows in over 500 updates. Terrain outside the bounds cannot cast shadows in this model.VattV_{\rm att}η\eta

    OrTeN uses a semi-empirical image formation model inspired by EO-NeRF’s shadow-fill and affine brightness approach . The predicted image for acquisition is[]27ii

    y^i=gi​[Vη​D+(1−Vη)​aamb​(𝐬)]​a¯+bi.\widehat{y}_{i}=g_{i}\bigl[V_{\eta}D+(1-V_{\eta})a_{\rm amb}(\mathbf{s})\bigr]\bar{a}+b_{i}.(10)

    The Sun-dependent ambient factor fills shadows without inheriting the direct-light angular response. Scalar gains and offsets absorb acquisition-wide brightness differences, with fixing the geometric mean gain to one across acquisitions. The same image model is used throughout training.aamb∈(0,1)a_{\rm amb}\in(0,1)gi=eui−u¯g_{i}=e^{u_{i}-\bar{u}}u¯=M−1​∑iui\bar{u}=M^{-1}\sum_{i}u_{i}MM

    Histogram-valley shadow detection  is adopted to provide an initial image-space shadow estimate at startup. Only sufficiently dark, distinct pixels are accepted, and mask erosion is applied to remove boundary transients. For an ordinary rendering batch , a regularizer is applied:[]1ℬ\mathcal{B}

    ℒshadow=|ℬ|−1​∑p∈ℬzp​Vp2,\mathcal{L}_{\rm shadow}=|\mathcal{B}|^{-1}\sum_{p\in\mathcal{B}}z_{p}V_{p}^{2},(11)

    where marks a detected core and means unknown. This loss is one-sided, so unlabeled pixels are not treated as either shadow or sunlit.zp=1z_{p}=1zp=0z_{p}=0

    3.3

    A linescan pixel has nominal origin and direction . Intrinsics and distortion are retained, and corrections are optimized in the local scene frame:(ℓ,s)(\ell,s)𝐨i0​(ℓ)\mathbf{o}_{i}^{0}(\ell)𝐝i0​(ℓ,s)\mathbf{d}_{i}^{0}(\ell,s)

    𝐨i\displaystyle\mathbf{o}_{i}=𝐨i0+Δ​𝐩i​(u),\displaystyle=\mathbf{o}_{i}^{0}+\Delta\mathbf{p}_{i}(u),(12)𝐝i\displaystyle\mathbf{d}_{i}=exp⁡([Δ​𝝎i​(u)]×)​𝐝i0,\displaystyle=\exp([\Delta\boldsymbol{\omega}_{i}(u)]_{\times})\mathbf{d}_{i}^{0},(13)Δ​𝐩i​(u)\displaystyle\Delta\mathbf{p}_{i}(u)=sp​∑k=03Bk​(u)​𝐏i​k,\displaystyle=s_{p}\sum_{k=0}^{3}B_{k}(u)\mathbf{P}_{ik},(14)Δ​𝝎i​(u)\displaystyle\Delta\boldsymbol{\omega}_{i}(u)=sω​[∑k=03Bk​(u)​𝐖i​k+r​𝐉i​(u)].\displaystyle=s_{\omega}\left[\sum_{k=0}^{3}B_{k}(u)\mathbf{W}_{ik}+r\mathbf{J}_{i}(u)\right].(15)

    Here is normalized acquisition time and are cubic Bernstein functions. The matrix implements the cross product with , and its exponential gives the corresponding rotation. The learned controls use physical scales which are constrained by soft priors based on expected trajectory error . During the refinement phase (), the ramp introduces angular jitter , represented by a cubic B-spline with 64 intervals per acquisition. Its global cubic component is removed so it cannot duplicate the smooth trajectory correction.u∈[0,1]u\in[0,1]BkB_{k}[𝝎]×[\boldsymbol{\omega}]_{\times}𝝎\boldsymbol{\omega}𝐏i​k,𝐖i​k\mathbf{P}_{ik},\mathbf{W}_{ik}sp,sωs_{p},s_{\omega}[]11Sec.3.5rr𝐉i\mathbf{J}_{i}

    3.4

    In addition to uniformly sampled rays, at each training iteration patches are sampled in source images and projected onto the current height field through the refined cameras. Each patch point is then projected from the surface into other acquisitions, where bilinear interpolation is used to calculate observed intensities. For accepted source–neighbor pairs, the normalized cross-correlation loss is5×55\times 5

    ℒNCC=𝔼P,i,j​[1−⟨Pi−P¯i,Pj−P¯j⟩‖Pi−P¯i‖2​‖Pj−P¯j‖2].\mathcal{L}_{\rm NCC}=\mathbb{E}_{P,i,j}\left[1-\frac{\langle P_{i}-\bar{P}_{i},P_{j}-\bar{P}_{j}\rangle}{\|P_{i}-\bar{P}_{i}\|_{2}\,\|P_{j}-\bar{P}_{j}\|_{2}}\right].(16)

    Here contain the observed patch intensities and are their means. is the inner product. Invalid, occluded, low-contrast, and nearly parallel view pairs are rejected, and up to three of the best eligible neighbors are retained per source patch. NCC is active in both roughing and refinement ().Pi,PjP_{i},P_{j}P¯i,P¯j\bar{P}_{i},\bar{P}_{j}⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangleSec.3.5

    3.5

    shows the overall network architecture. Training progresses from images downsampled by to , then to native resolution. Active encoding levels are adjusted to approximately match the current image resolution. There are two training stages: roughing and refinement. Roughing ends when terrain and camera motion stabilize or the roughing update limit is reached. Refinement lowers the geometry learning rate, increases NCC sampling, and introduces jitter and local regularization.Fig.34×4\times2×2\times

    Let be the RMS brightness of all training pixels. The rendering loss issy=𝔼train​[y2]s_{y}=\sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{\rm train}[y^{2}]}

    ℒI/F=𝔼p∈ℬ​[(y^p−yp)2/sy2].\mathcal{L}_{I/F}=\mathbb{E}_{p\in\mathcal{B}}\left[(\widehat{y}_{p}-y_{p})^{2}/s_{y}^{2}\right].(17)

    Albedo starts exactly at , ambient at 0.2, and gains and offsets at one and zero. The remaining surface and appearance penalties aresys_{y}

    ℒbend\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\rm bend}=𝔼𝐱​[sh2​‖𝐇sh​hθ​(𝐱)‖F2],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}}\left[s_{h}^{2}\|\mathbf{H}_{s_{h}}h_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})\|_{F}^{2}\right],(18)ℒwidth\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\rm width}=log⁡(1+(β/g0)2),\displaystyle=\log\bigl(1+(\beta/g_{0})^{2}\bigr),(19)ℒradio\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\rm radio}=𝔼i​[((ui−u¯)/0.1)2+(bi/0.01)2],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{i}\left[((u_{i}-\bar{u})/0.1)^{2}+(b_{i}/0.01)^{2}\right],(20)ℒamb\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\rm amb}=𝔼𝐬​[[logit⁡aamb​(𝐬)−log⁡9]+2].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{s}}\left[\bigl[\operatorname{logit}a_{\rm amb}(\mathbf{s})-\log 9\bigr]_{+}^{2}\right].(21)

    Here is the finite-difference Hessian. In order, these losses regularize surface bending, control the rendering width, enforce radiometric calibration, and constrain the ambient illumination. The fixed scale is the initial training-image GSD. The optional ambient penalty acts only when the ambient factor exceeds 0.9.𝐇sh\mathbf{H}_{s_{h}}g0g_{0}

    Camera regularization penalizes the dimensionless trajectory controls and, in refinement, the sampled jitter motion. Let concatenate the trajectory position and rotation corrections divided by and . Its second derivative penalizes trajectory curvature:𝐜i​(u)\mathbf{c}_{i}(u)sps_{p}sωs_{\omega}

    ℒcamera=\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\rm camera}={}λC​𝔼i,k​(‖𝐏i​k‖22+‖𝐖i​k‖22)\displaystyle\lambda_{C}\mathbb{E}_{i,k}(\|\mathbf{P}_{ik}\|_{2}^{2}+\|\mathbf{W}_{ik}\|_{2}^{2})+λC​𝟏r>0​𝔼i,u​‖𝐉i​(u)‖22\displaystyle+\lambda_{C}\mathbf{1}_{r>0}\mathbb{E}_{i,u}\|\mathbf{J}_{i}(u)\|_{2}^{2}+λK𝔼i∫01∥𝐜i′′(u)∥22du.\displaystyle+\lambda_{K}\mathbb{E}_{i}\int_{0}^{1}\|\mathbf{c}_{i}^{\prime\prime}(u)\|_{2}^{2}du.(22)

    For each camera or solar ray, the proposal loss is the histogram-envelope objective used by Nerfstudio :[]35

    ℒenv=∑l𝔼j​[wj−Wl​j]+2wj+10−7.\mathcal{L}_{\rm env}=\sum_{l}\mathbb{E}_{j}\frac{[w_{j}-W_{lj}]_{+}^{2}}{w_{j}+10^{-7}}.(23)

    Here is proposal level ’s total mass in bins overlapping final interval . The camera and solar proposal losses are summed as . The complete objective isWl​jW_{lj}lljjℒproposal\mathcal{L}_{\rm proposal}

    ℒ=\displaystyle\mathcal{L}={}ℒI/F+η​λN​ℒNCC+λW​ℒwidth+λR​ℒradio\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{I/F}+\eta\lambda_{N}\mathcal{L}_{\rm NCC}+\lambda_{W}\mathcal{L}_{\rm width}+\lambda_{R}\mathcal{L}_{\rm radio}+ℒcamera+ℒproposal\displaystyle+\mathcal{L}_{\rm camera}+\mathcal{L}_{\rm proposal}+r⁡(λB​ℒbend+λS​ℒshadow+λA​ℒamb).\displaystyle+r\left(\lambda_{B}\mathcal{L}_{\rm bend}+\lambda_{S}\mathcal{L}_{\rm shadow}+\lambda_{A}\mathcal{L}_{\rm amb}\right).(24)

    The refinement ramp is zero during roughing and rises over 500 updates after transition.rr

    4

    4.1

    Four lunar and Martian datasets were selected for their varied terrain and illumination and the availability of reference DTMs. Jezero Crater, Gale Crater, and Olympus Mons each contain fifteen CTX crops. McGetchin Crater contains ten LROC NAC crops of the same size. Images are calibrated to I/F using the Integrated Software for Imagers and Spectrometers (ISIS) and paired with initial line-scan camera states. gives additional details on the instruments and reference DTM quality for each dataset. The Olympus dataset reference uses a DTM separately reconstructed from the same image collection because a high-quality engineering DTM was unavailable.1024×10241024\times 1024Table1

    4.2

    Metrics for each scene are calculated over a fixed reference footprint that is covered by at least five initial cameras. To resolve the gauge freedom inherent in the bundle adjustment process, reconstructed DTMs are aligned to the reference DTM using a six-degree-of-freedom rigid transformation. No scale change, local warping, or separate alignment for different metrics is applied. For aligned height errors on valid posts, the metrics areep=h^a​(p)−href​(p)e_{p}=\widehat{h}_{a}(p)-h_{\rm ref}(p)NN

    RMSEa=N−1​∑pep2,MAEa=N−1​∑p|ep|.\mathrm{RMSE}_{a}=\sqrt{N^{-1}\sum_{p}e_{p}^{2}},\qquad\mathrm{MAE}_{a}=N^{-1}\sum_{p}|e_{p}|.(25)

    The subscript denotes metrics applied to rigidly aligned DTMs, so these scores measure relative shape rather than absolute geolocation.aa

    Slope is evaluated using a local quadratic surface fit calculated over a sliding window. This follows established practices in terrain analysis  and reduces sensitivity to reference DTM artifacts. Slope RMSE is the RMS difference between slope angles in degrees, under the same rigid alignment. Although OrTeN permits direct network differentiation, the reported comparison differentiates polynomial fits to every method’s raster export to match spatial scale. Height RMSE and MAE use unsmoothed elevations.9×99\times 9[]18a

    One block per acquisition, at the full image resolution, is held out during training for perceptural metric calculation. This is necessary because of learned image-dependent radiometric calibration. PSNR is where is the 99th minus 1st percentile of the pooled held-out observations per scene. SSIM uses the same range and Gaussian windows ( pixels), averaged over valid window centers.64×6464\times 6410​log10⁡(R2/MSE)10\log_{10}(R^{2}/\mathrm{MSE})RR11×1111\times 11σ=1.5\sigma=1.5

    4.3

    All training runs use a single seed, are limited to 15,000 iterations, and use a batch size of 8,192 rays. The same configuration for OrTeN is used across all four scenes. This includes enabling trajectory BA, jitter adjustment, and the detected-shadow prior with weight 0.01. The roughing stage iteration cap is set to 8,000 updates.

    Comparisons with depth-supervised EO-NeRF  and ASP  are reported. EO-NeRF uses the same camera-derived scene bounds as OrTeN, 8,192 rays per update, 128 depth samples per ray, and fixed cameras. Its depth targets come from the unaligned ASP stereo mosaics, without reference-terrain supervision or registration. ASP uses image-based BA, dense stereo, and jitter refinement anchored to its own stereo terrain estimates. The same ASP pipeline is used for all scenes.[]27[]7

    Mean setup-plus-training times are 52.7/41.2 minutes for OrTeN on NVIDIA RTX 6000 Ada Generation/RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs, respectively. These include periodic evaluation and checkpointing, exclude final evaluation, and average different scene/configuration mixes across GPUs. OrTeN uses Adam with a 500-step warmup to learning rates of for geometry and appearance, for cameras, and for proposal networks. Geometry decays during roughing, then starts refinement at most and decays to . Appearance and camera rates finish at and .3×10−33\times 10^{-3}10−310^{-3}10−210^{-2}1.5×10−41.5\times 10^{-4}5×10−55\times 10^{-5}3×10−43\times 10^{-4}10−510^{-5}

    4.4

    gives the results of the baseline OrTeN configuration on each scene. OrTeN attains sub-GSD height RMSE in Jezero, Gale, and McGetchin scenes. On the Olympus Mons scene, the RMSE remains at 2.91 GSD. Its large relief (almost 3 km) and substantial cast shadows make reconstruction challenging. The lack of an independent, high-accuracy reference limits comparison with ASP, which performs similarly on this scene.Tab.2aa×\times

    Depth-supervised EO-NeRF fails to reconstruct accurate DTMs in any of the scenes despite access to structural supervision. It falls short of OrTeN both visually and in structural accuracy. Noting that the default EO-NeRF configuration trains for much longer (300,000 iterations) and takes 10-20 hours to converge, this comparison demonstrates that OrTeN’s approach achieves meaningful improvement in both efficiency and accuracy.

    ASP recovers sound DTMs for all four scenes, but performs worse than OrTeN on all scenes except Olympus Mons. as opposed to ASP, which typically processes images pairwise or in smaller subsets. OrTeN also benefits from its semi-empirical appearance modeling which allows it to better deal with shadows and varying illumination conditions which may confound feature matching in purely photogrammetric approaches.

    Four ablation studies were conducted to evaluate the impact of the three key features in this work: bundle adjustment with jitter, normalized cross-correlation (NCC) for photometric consistency, and semi-empirical appearance modeling with shadow modeling. The results of the ablation are summarized in .Tab.3

    Removing BA significantly degrades the quality of the reconstructed DTMs across all scenes, highlighting the importance of joint optimization of camera parameters and scene geometry. shows baseline and no-BA renderings of the same acquisition for the McGetchin Crater scene. The no-BA ablation shows clearly degraded visual reconstruction quality with a drop of more than 10 dB in reserved-pixel PSNR. The DTM is similarly impacted with RMSE increasing from 0.43 to 10.36 m and the quality of the reconstruction visibly degrading, especially in the fine detail around the central crater region.Fig.4a

    Disabling NCC has an even more pronounced effect on the quality of the reconstructed DTMs. shows baseline and no-NCC renderings of the same acquisition for the Jezero Crater scene, and again illustrates the degradation of fine detail around the crater region. In some of the scenes, the PSNR improves in the no-NCC ablation compared to the baseline. Rendering loss alone can therefore be misleading when assessing terrain reconstruction, especially in low-disparity orbital scenes.Fig.5

    Removal of geometric shadows produces a less pronounced effect on the quality of the reconstructed DTMs compared to the other ablations, but can be observed in reconstruction quality. shows baseline and no-shadow renderings of the same acquisition for the Olympus Mons scene. The baseline is able to reconstruct the large shadow cast by the cliff face while the ablated scene cannot.Fig.6

    5

    OrTeN jointly reconstructs terrain and refines line-scan cameras from calibrated orbital images without depth supervision or stereo initialization. Across four Mars and Moon scenes, it achieves sub-GSD aligned terrain RMSE in three and improves on the tested ASP reconstruction in those same three scenes. The ablations demonstrate the importance of camera refinement and surface-patch NCC for achieving high geometric accuracy. They also show that an accurate image reconstruction can coexist with an incorrect surface. Comparison with EO-NeRF with depth supervision also demonstrates that structural priors are not sufficient to achieve accurate terrain reconstruction efficiently.

    However, a number of limitations remain. Without structural priors such as ranging measurements or known control points, absolute geolocation is not possible. Furthermore, it is possible that integrating structural priors into OrTeN could improve reconstruction accuracy and efficiency and should be tested. While the height map representation is an effective structural prior for the datasets considered here, when detail becomes sufficient, this representation becomes more limiting. For instance, height maps cannot represent overhangs or complex 3D structures like caves. Future work should work on mitigating these shortcomings to allow ground level imagery to be integrated into the terrain reconstruction process.
